sources.note: S0679's critique of an uploaded framework document (Observation->Evidence->Fact->Comparison->Rule/Logic->Justification->Knowledge, with P(F|I) and (F_{<=t},S_t,R_t)->K_t): argues the framework's listed 'invariants' are not proven invariants but merely dimensions along which frameworks differ, that a common algebraic structure is premature, that epistemic state may be multidimensional (proposition/support/justification/status/uncertainty/time), and that Determination D_t(p) -- the operation (O,E,F_{<t},C,R)->D_t(p) -- is the missing explicit mathematical object needed before invariance can responsibly be discussed. Related to but distinct from determination-lineage-invariant (S0678, which emphasizes provenance/reconstruction of why p was determined) -- this document emphasizes Determination as a first-class formal object/operation in its own right. Per the git history, this brainstorming later becomes formalized as MD-104's 'Determination is the missing mathematical object' framing.

rows.anchor: O_t -> E_t(p|C,M) -> R_t(p|E,F,C,M) -> D_t(p) -> F_t ... Determination is the missing mathematical object in the current framework.
rows.statement: Proposes the full research pipeline O_t -> E_t(p|C,M) -> R_t(p|E,F,C,M) -> D_t(p) -> F_t (observation, conditional evidence assessment, conditional reasoning, determination, fact), identifying D_t as the determination and concluding that Determination is the missing mathematical object in the current framework, since the prior pipeline treated Observation->Evidence->Fact as deterministic rather than making each stage explicitly conditional on context/time/model/rules/assumptions.
missing: formal definition of the determination operation D_t itself

lineage_claims.quote: we have now discovered that the proposed sequence is still too simple

rows.anchor: P(F\mid O_t,C_t,M_t,F_{<t},A_t) where A_t represents assumptions. This is not a recommendation that the Kernel should store this probability. It is a research question about what the probabilistic regime needs.
rows.statement: The framework's P(F|O) is too simplistic because the same observation can support different propositions depending on context, interpretation, prior facts, model, measurement method, source reliability, time, and assumptions; proposes P(F|O_t,C_t,M_t,F_{<t},A_t) instead, explicitly framed as a research question about probabilistic-regime requirements, not a Kernel storage recommendation.

lineage_claims.quote: P(F\mid O)  is too simplistic

rows.anchor: certainty of the rule != certainty of its premises != certainty of the conclusion. This is precisely the combination problem that the framework identifies but hasn't yet solved.
rows.statement: Challenges the framework's use of the word 'established' for facts feeding logic/rules: a fact can have a graded epistemic state (e.g. P(F1)=0.8) even while the logical rule F1 and F2 => K applying to it is completely valid; therefore certainty of the rule, certainty of its premises, and certainty of the conclusion are three distinct things -- this is the combination problem the framework identifies but has not yet solved.
missing: a solution to the combination problem
invariants: rule certainty, premise certainty, and conclusion certainty are three distinct quantities

rows.anchor: Layer 1 -- uncertainty in extraction: O -> F, e.g. P(F|O)=0.8. Layer 2 -- uncertainty propagated through reasoning: given P(F1)=0.8 and F1=>K, we need to determine the epistemic state of K. ... How does uncertainty in premises interact with logical structure?
rows.statement: Identifies two distinct uncertainty layers: Layer 1, uncertainty in extraction (O->F, e.g. P(F|O)=0.8), and Layer 2, uncertainty propagated through reasoning (given P(F1)=0.8 and a rule F1=>K, the epistemic state of K is not automatically P(K)=0.8 and requires a combination semantics); the real underlying problem is how uncertainty in premises interacts with logical structure -- more fundamental than choosing among Bayesian/fuzzy/Dempster-Shafer.
missing: the combination semantics itself

rows.anchor: uncertainty representation; conditional structure; combination rule; temporal aspect; conflict handling; ignorance representation. I would not call these invariants. They are dimensions along which the frameworks differ. ... We need a stricter definition of invariant: I(X)=I(Y) under some legitimate transformation between representations.
rows.statement: Challenges the framework's list of cross-framework commonalities (uncertainty representation, conditional structure, combination rule, temporal aspect, conflict handling, ignorance representation) being called 'invariants': since Bayesian != Dempster-Shafer != Fuzzy != Argumentation in their uncertainty semantics, 'all frameworks represent uncertainty' establishes only a common research concern, not a mathematical invariant. Proposes the stricter test: an invariant must satisfy I(X)=I(Y) under some legitimate transformation between representations.
invariants: a genuine invariant requires I(X)=I(Y) under a legitimate transformation, not merely a shared research theme

lineage_claims.target: the uploaded framework's list of cross-framework 'invariants'
lineage_claims.quote: I would not call these invariants.

rows.anchor: There may be a common algebraic structure underlying all these frameworks, e.g. lattice or measure-theoretic structure. I would mark this highly speculative. ... P(p) and mu(p) and mu_fuzzy(p) and Acceptable(p) may not be representations of one common mathematical object. They could represent different epistemic properties.
rows.statement: Marks the framework's proposed 'common algebraic structure' (e.g. a lattice or measure-theoretic structure unifying all evidence-combination frameworks) as highly speculative and premature: before seeking a common algebra one must establish that the objects being represented (P(p), mu(p), mu_fuzzy(p), Acceptable(p)) are actually the same kind of thing -- they could instead represent different epistemic properties, which is exactly the danger the research has been trying to avoid.

lineage_claims.quote: I would mark this highly speculative.

rows.anchor: First: What is the epistemic object? Second: What is the determination operation? Third: What does each regime represent? Fourth: When can two representations be considered equivalent? Fifth: What survives those equivalences? Only then do we ask: What is invariant?
rows.statement: Proposes a safer six-step research ordering before asking about invariance: first, what is the epistemic object; second, what is the determination operation; third, what does each regime represent; fourth, when can two representations be considered equivalent; fifth, what survives those equivalences; only then, what is invariant.
invariants: invariance must not be asked before the epistemic object and determination operation are defined

rows.anchor: E_t(p)=(proposition, support, justification, status, uncertainty, time). ... Bayesian theory may primarily represent uncertainty. Argumentation represents support/attack. Non-monotonic logic represents defeasible status. Epistemic logic represents knowledge relations. Temporal logic represents temporal truth. Measurement theory represents numerical attributes. These may be different dimensions of an epistemic state, rather than competing representations of one scalar object.
rows.statement: Hypothesizes that epistemic state itself needs decomposition rather than being a generic scalar output E in script-E: E_t(p)=(proposition,support,justification,status,uncertainty,time). Under this hypothesis, different mathematical frameworks may each be capturing a different DIMENSION of epistemic state rather than competing representations of one scalar object: Bayesian theory primarily represents uncertainty, argumentation represents support/attack, non-monotonic logic represents defeasible status, epistemic logic represents knowledge relations, temporal logic represents temporal truth, and measurement theory represents numerical attributes. Explicitly framed as a hypothesis needing testing, not a proposed Kernel model.
missing: testing of the hypothesis

rows.anchor: How should conditional evidence and conditional reasoning combine to produce an epistemic state? I would retain that. But add: What are the distinct components of the epistemic state being produced? And then: Which components are regime-specific and which are regime-independent?
rows.statement: Extends the central research question: retains 'how should conditional evidence and conditional reasoning combine to produce an epistemic state', and adds two further questions -- what are the distinct components of the epistemic state being produced, and which components are regime-specific versus regime-independent.

rows.anchor: Is Knowledge probabilistic? No. Is the extraction of Knowledge probabilistic? Some extraction processes are probabilistic. Is the resulting epistemic state probabilistic? It can be represented probabilistically, but that is regime-dependent. ... What exactly is being represented by the probability?
rows.statement: Traces the evolving answer to a recurring question across the discussion: 'Is Knowledge probabilistic?' -> No; 'Is the extraction of Knowledge probabilistic?' -> some extraction processes are; 'Is the resulting epistemic state probabilistic?' -> it can be represented probabilistically, but that is regime-dependent; the deeper open question that now emerges is 'What exactly is being represented by the probability?'

rows.anchor: What is observed? -> Observation. What makes it evidence? -> Evidence relation. ... What does probability represent? -> Unknown -- investigate. ... Are these actually different lenses on one epistemic state, or are they lenses on different dimensions of it?
rows.statement: Proposes replacing an immediate 11-framework comparison with a 16-row question/research-target matrix (what is observed->Observation; what makes it evidence->Evidence relation; evidence for what->Proposition/hypothesis; what makes a proposition determined->Determination; what makes determination legitimate->Reasoning/justification; what can be uncertain->Observation/proposition/model/inference; what can be revised->Determination/conclusion/state; what does time change->Validity/evidence/state; what does probability represent->Unknown, investigate; what does logic represent->Inference structure; what does argumentation represent->Support/attack; what does fuzzy value represent->Truth/vagueness; what does D-S represent->Evidence/ignorance; what does epistemic logic represent->Knowledge relation; what does temporal logic represent->Temporal properties; what does measurement theory represent->Empirical-to-numerical representation), then asks whether these are different lenses on one epistemic state or lenses on different dimensions of it.

rows.anchor: Strong: correctly separates probability from Knowledge; correctly identifies conditional evidence; correctly identifies conditional reasoning; correctly keeps this as research rather than architecture; correctly demands cross-framework comparison. Needs correction: P(F|O) is too simplistic; "established facts" should not automatically be treated as deterministic; the listed common properties are not yet proven invariants; the common algebraic structure is premature; epistemic state may be multidimensional; determination is currently missing as an explicit mathematical object.
rows.statement: Gives an explicit verdict on the uploaded framework document: five strong points (correctly separates probability from Knowledge; correctly identifies conditional evidence; correctly identifies conditional reasoning; correctly keeps this as research rather than architecture; correctly demands cross-framework comparison) and six points needing correction (P(F|O) too simplistic; 'established facts' should not automatically be treated as deterministic; listed common properties are not yet proven invariants; the common algebraic structure is premature; epistemic state may be multidimensional; determination is currently missing as an explicit mathematical object). Also explicitly agrees with the framework's constraint: 'Do not design the Kernel. Do not change its boundary. Challenge the architecture; do not become its architect.'
invariants: challenge the architecture; do not become its architect

rows.anchor: (O, E, F_{<t}, C, R) -> D_t(p) where D_t(p) is the determination of proposition p at time t. Then we investigate how D_t(p) is represented by probability, logic, Dempster-Shafer, argumentation, fuzzy logic, etc. I think that is the next missing piece before we can responsibly talk about the invariant.
rows.statement: Proposes continuing research at exactly one point: formalizing '(O,E,F_{<t},C,R) -> D_t(p)' as the operation producing the determination of proposition p at time t, then investigating how D_t(p) is represented by probability, logic, Dempster-Shafer, argumentation, fuzzy logic, etc. -- framed as the next missing piece before responsibly discussing invariance.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS needs to determine what the organization should currently accept as knowledge, based on incomplete and sometimes conflicting information, and it must be able to explain and revise that determination later. ... Information -> What did we actually observe? -> ... -> What can we defend as "knowledge"?
rows.statement: States the business problem in one sentence: KnowledgeOS needs to determine what the organization should currently accept as knowledge, based on incomplete and sometimes conflicting information, and must be able to explain and revise that determination later; there is no direct pipeline from information to knowledge -- it passes through what was observed, what the observation means, what evidence it provides, evidence strength, existing facts/evidence, applicable rules, conflicts, current conclusion, and finally what can be defended as knowledge, with every step conditional and imperfect.

rows.anchor: Port 8081 is open. That's an observation. Does it prove Nexus is available? No. It is evidence supporting that possibility. ... another process uses the port; the service is running but inaccessible from the required network; the information is outdated; this is not the production server. So: Observation != Evidence != Fact.
rows.statement: Problem 1 (Information is not automatically evidence): 'Port 8081 is open' is an observation, not proof that Nexus is available -- it is evidence supporting that possibility only, since alternative explanations exist (another process on the port, network-inaccessible service, outdated information, wrong server); therefore Observation != Evidence != Fact.
invariants: Observation, Evidence, and Fact are three distinct things

rows.anchor: Observation A -> supports "Nexus is running"; Observation B -> supports "Nexus is reachable"; Observation C -> contradicts "Nexus is reachable from production". Now what? We have conflicting evidence. The system must determine: What should we currently conclude? This is the determination problem.
rows.statement: Problem 2 (evidence does not automatically create a fact): three observations produce conflicting evidence (A supports 'Nexus is running', B supports 'Nexus is reachable', C contradicts 'Nexus is reachable from production'); the system must determine what to currently conclude -- this is the determination problem.

rows.anchor: A system is "migration ready" only if: dependencies are identified; network access is verified; backup is verified; certificates are understood; rollback is defined. ... Dependencies: Strong, Network: Strong, Backup: Uncertain, Certificates: Missing, Rollback: Strong. Can we say "Migration ready"? Not simply by looking at the data. We need the rule for determining readiness.
rows.statement: Problem 3 (the rules for determining something matter): given a five-criterion migration-readiness policy (dependencies/network/backup/certificates/rollback) and mixed evidence strength per criterion (Strong/Strong/Uncertain/Missing/Strong), whether 'migration ready' can be asserted cannot be read off the data alone -- an explicit rule for determining readiness is required.

rows.anchor: Architect A says: "80% confidence is sufficient. Proceed." Architect B says: "The certificate dependency is unknown. Therefore readiness cannot be established." Both have the same information. But they use different reasoning criteria. ... KnowledgeOS should probably not decide which reasoning system is universally correct. It should preserve enough information so that the appropriate reasoning regime can make its determination.
rows.statement: Problem 4 (different reasoning methods can produce different answers): two architects viewing identical evidence reach opposite conclusions (Architect A: '80% confidence is sufficient, proceed' vs Architect B: 'certificate dependency unknown, therefore readiness cannot be established') because they apply different reasoning criteria (Bayesian probability vs logical derivation vs argumentation vs Dempster-Shafer belief+ignorance vs non-monotonic defeasible conclusions); principle derived: KnowledgeOS should probably not decide which reasoning system is universally correct, but should preserve enough information for the appropriate reasoning regime to make its own determination.
invariants: KnowledgeOS never privileges one reasoning system as universally correct

rows.anchor: We don't yet know what "knowledge" actually is ... Is a highly probable conclusion knowledge? Is a logically derived conclusion knowledge? Is an institutionally approved statement knowledge? Is something knowledge if nobody can explain why it is true? Is an old fact still knowledge after it becomes obsolete? Is "unknown" itself part of knowledge? These are not implementation questions yet. They are domain-definition questions.
rows.statement: Problem 6 (we don't yet know what 'knowledge' actually is), the deepest of the six: facts, evidence, observations, justification, reasoning, probability, belief, commitments, conclusions, and knowledge have not yet had their boundaries rigorously established; poses six unresolved domain-definition questions (is a highly probable conclusion knowledge; is a logically derived conclusion knowledge; is an institutionally approved statement knowledge; is something knowledge if nobody can explain why it is true; is an old, obsolete fact still knowledge; is 'unknown' itself part of knowledge) -- explicitly framed as domain-definition questions, not implementation questions.

rows.anchor: Information -> Evidence -> Reasoning -> Determination -> Knowledge ... contextual; time-dependent; incomplete; sometimes probabilistic; sometimes logical; sometimes argumentative; sometimes governed by explicit rules.
rows.statement: Summarizes the business problem as a transformation from Information to Defensible Knowledge via Information->Evidence->Reasoning->Determination->Knowledge, where the transformation is contextual, time-dependent, incomplete, and sometimes probabilistic, logical, argumentative, or governed by explicit rules.

rows.anchor: We are not trying to make KnowledgeOS a probability engine. We are asking: What is happening when an organization turns incomplete information into a defensible determination? Probability is one possible tool. Logic is another. Argumentation is another. Measurement theory is another. Temporal logic is another. They are lenses for parts of the process.
rows.statement: Reframes why the mathematics research exists: not to make KnowledgeOS a probability engine, but to answer 'what is happening when an organization turns incomplete information into a defensible determination?' -- probability, logic, argumentation, measurement theory, and temporal logic are each lenses for parts of that process, not competing definitions of it.

rows.anchor: Level 1 -- Business problem: How do we know what we currently know? Level 2 -- Scientific problem: How does incomplete, conditional and conflicting evidence become a justified determination? Level 3 -- KnowledgeOS problem: What minimum information must be preserved so that those determinations can be reconstructed, challenged and revised using different reasoning methods? And we are currently working on Level 2. We should not jump to Level 3 and define the Kernel yet.
rows.statement: Structures the research into three levels: Level 1 Business problem (how do we know what we currently know), Level 2 Scientific problem (how does incomplete/conditional/conflicting evidence become a justified determination), Level 3 KnowledgeOS problem (what minimum information must be preserved so determinations can be reconstructed/challenged/revised using different reasoning methods); explicitly states the research is currently at Level 2 and should not jump to Level 3 to define the Kernel yet -- the reason for repeatedly stopping premature Kernel-tuple writing. Next concrete target: understand the exact boundary between INFORMATION -> EVIDENCE -> REASONING -> DETERMINATION -> KNOWLEDGE before asking what KnowledgeOS/the Kernel must preserve/guarantee.
invariants: do not define the Kernel (Level 3) before the Level 2 scientific boundary questions are resolved

rows.anchor: We have solved a substantial part of the conceptual problem, but we have not yet solved the formal definition of Knowledge or the Kernel. ... I would say we have solved perhaps 60-70% of the conceptual framing, but only 20-30% of the formal problem.
rows.statement: Self-assessed research status: roughly 60-70% of the conceptual framing has been solved, but only 20-30% of the formal mathematical problem; the biggest achievement is not a definition but locating the problem correctly.

rows.anchor: Knowledge != probability: Strong. Information != knowledge: Strong. Knowledge changes with time: Strong. ... One universal ideal state: Not established. Knowledge as subset of ideal state: Interesting but unproven. Infinite Knowledge Space: Useful hypothesis, undefined. ... Epistemic equivalence: Unresolved. Minimum substrate: Not solved. KnowledgeOS Kernel: Not ready to define.
rows.statement: Gives an 18-row status table rating each research claim from this thread: strongly established (Knowledge!=probability, Information!=knowledge, Knowledge changes with time, observation is context/comparison dependent, probability as an uncertainty regime, dimension uncertainty, value uncertainty, multiple kinds of knowledge), strong hypothesis (reference/ideal state is important), interesting-but-unproven or useful-but-undefined (knowledge as subset of ideal state, infinite Knowledge Space, determination, fact-as-determination), and not established/rejected/unresolved (one universal ideal state, probability as universal extraction mechanism, epistemic equivalence, minimum substrate, KnowledgeOS Kernel -- explicitly 'not ready to define').

rows.anchor: Descriptive: Nexus version is 2.69. Evaluative: Nexus 2.69 is outdated. Normative: Nexus must run 3.85. Inferential: Because A and B, C follows. Probabilistic: There is 80% support for C. Historical: Nexus was version 2.69 on 1 August. We should not assume all of these are identical objects. ... Knowledge is a family of epistemic determinations, rather than one homogeneous object.
rows.statement: Identifies six distinguishable kinds of knowledge statement -- descriptive, evaluative, normative, inferential, probabilistic, historical -- with examples, and hypothesizes that Knowledge is a family of epistemic determinations rather than one homogeneous object; explicitly unresolved but increasingly important.
missing: proof or disproof that these six kinds require genuinely different treatment

rows.anchor: what its inputs are; what its output is; when it is valid; when it is justified; whether it can be probabilistic; whether it can be partial; whether it can be contradictory; how it changes over time; how it differs from belief; how it differs from hypothesis; how it becomes a fact; how it can be challenged. This is probably the single most important unresolved conceptual problem.
rows.statement: Names 'what is a determination?' as the single most important unresolved conceptual problem in the thread, listing twelve unanswered sub-questions: its inputs, its output, when it is valid, when it is justified, whether it can be probabilistic, whether it can be partial, whether it can be contradictory, how it changes over time, how it differs from belief, how it differs from hypothesis, how it becomes a fact, and how it can be challenged.

rows.anchor: Initially we were asking: "What should KnowledgeOS store?" That was too early. We are now asking: "How does an observer move from an incompletely known, potentially unbounded state space to a defensible determination about a subject at a particular point in time?" ... Dimension discovery + Information extraction + Comparison + Reasoning + Determination + Temporal revision.
rows.statement: Identifies the biggest achievement as locating the problem, not defining it: the research question shifted from the premature 'what should KnowledgeOS store?' to 'how does an observer move from an incompletely known, potentially unbounded state space to a defensible determination about a subject at a particular point in time?', underpinned by Dimension discovery + Information extraction + Comparison + Reasoning + Determination + Temporal revision.

rows.anchor: I would not add another 20 concepts to KnowledgeOS. Instead, I would test our theory with real cases. Take three radically different cases: Case 1 -- Descriptive ... Case 2 -- Evaluative ... Case 3 -- Predictive ... If the same conceptual machinery works across them, we have evidence. If it doesn't, we have discovered that Knowledge is not one mechanism.
rows.statement: Imposes discipline against further ontology expansion: rather than adding more concepts, test the theory against three radically different worked cases (Case 1 descriptive: 'Nexus is running version 2.69'; Case 2 evaluative: 'Nexus 2.69 is not acceptable'; Case 3 predictive: 'Nexus will probably fail under condition X'), documenting for each what was observed, assumed/discovered dimensions, prior knowledge, reference state, rules, uncertainty, determination, timing, and revision conditions; if the same conceptual machinery works across all three, that is evidence for the model, and if not, Knowledge is not one mechanism.
missing: execution of the proposed three-case test

experiment.hypothesis: the same conceptual machinery (dimension discovery, extraction, comparison, reasoning, determination) explains descriptive, evaluative, and predictive knowledge alike
experiment.setup: three worked cases, one per kind
experiment.assumptions: unstated
experiment.inputs: three example propositions
experiment.method: document a fixed template of questions per case and compare results
experiment.result: not yet run
experiment.interpretation: unstated
experiment.limitations: unstated
experiment.conclusion: proposed as the next concrete test before further ontology expansion

rows.anchor: The two hardest unresolved questions are now: 1. How is the relevant dimension space discovered? and: 2. What exactly constitutes a valid epistemic determination? I would research those two questions next. And only after that would I return to measure theory and ask: Which parts of this process genuinely require measure-theoretic probability, and which do not? That prevents us from making the mathematics drive the ontology.
rows.statement: Names the two hardest unresolved questions to research next: (1) how is the relevant dimension space discovered, and (2) what exactly constitutes a valid epistemic determination; only after resolving those should the research return to measure theory and ask which parts of the process genuinely require measure-theoretic probability and which do not -- explicitly to prevent the mathematics from driving the ontology.
invariants: mathematics must never be allowed to drive the ontology; the ontology question is resolved first

rows.anchor: Q13: What makes information become Knowledge? ... evidence? probability threshold? logical proof? trusted authority? reproducibility? governance decision? consensus? ... Q14: Is Knowledge always true? ... Q15: What is the relationship between Knowledge and Truth? ... We should not assume Knowledge=Truth. ... Q16: What is the role of belief? ... Q17: What is evidence? ... Q18: What is justification? ... Q19: What is a determination? Determination: (O,E,R,C,t) -> K. But this is only a placeholder. We don't know the correct arguments or semantics.
rows.statement: Poses seven unresolved questions at the core of the epistemic vocabulary: Q13 what makes information become Knowledge (candidate criteria: evidence, probability threshold, logical proof, trusted authority, reproducibility, governance decision, consensus -- possibly domain-dependent); Q14 is Knowledge always true (partially resolved via temporal indexing, formally undefined); Q15 the relationship between Knowledge and Truth (Knowledge subset Truth? Knowledge approx Justified Determination? Knowledge=Representation of believed truth? -- explicitly should not assume Knowledge=Truth); Q16 the role of belief vs hypothesis/assumption/trust/confidence/determination/fact/knowledge ('we believe X is required' != 'X is required'); Q17 what evidence is (is it information? always observable? can a determination be evidence for another? does it have strength/context/conflict/expiry?); Q18 what justification is (deductive/inductive/statistical/authority/law/precedent/measurement/argumentation/causal -- regime-dependent); Q19 what a determination is, formalized only as a placeholder Determination:(O,E,R,C,t)->K, with the correct arguments and semantics unknown -- named a major unresolved question.
missing: formal semantics of the Determination operator

rows.anchor: What is the State? -> What are its Dimensions? -> Which Dimensions are Relevant? -> What are their Ideal/Reference Values? -> What can be Observed? -> How is Information Extracted? -> How is Evidence evaluated? -> How is Reasoning performed? -> How is a Determination established? -> When does Determination become Knowledge? -> How is Knowledge revised over Time? -> What must be preserved? -> What is Kernel-essential? ... We have made meaningful progress through roughly the middle of this chain. The bottom half is still unresolved.
rows.statement: Represents the whole research problem as a 13-step chain: State -> Dimensions -> Relevant Dimensions -> Ideal/Reference Values -> Observable -> Information Extraction -> Evidence Evaluation -> Reasoning -> Determination -> Determination-becomes-Knowledge -> Revision over Time -> What must be preserved -> Kernel-essential; self-assesses that meaningful progress has been made through roughly the middle of the chain, with the bottom half (determination onward) still unresolved.

rows.anchor: Q1: What is a dimension? Working answer: A fact/aspect of a state. Next: Test against many domains. Q2: What is a determination? This is the biggest gap. Q3: What does completeness mean? Not "How many facts do we have?" but: How can we determine whether our identified dimensions and their values are sufficiently complete to characterize the state for a given purpose at a given time? Q3 is where dimension uncertainty and probability work will become most important.
rows.statement: Names three priority research questions: (1) what is a dimension (working answer: a fact/aspect of a state; next step: test across many domains for mathematical coherence); (2) what is a determination (the biggest gap: how does information about dimensions become a justified statement about the state); (3) what does completeness mean, reframed from 'how many facts do we have' to 'how can we determine whether identified dimensions and their values are sufficiently complete to characterize the state for a given purpose at a given time' -- explicitly flagged as where dimension uncertainty and probability work will matter most.

rows.anchor: Knowledge is not yet formally defined. Knowledge Space is not yet formally defined. Ideal State is not yet formally defined. Dimension is a working concept. Observation is a working concept. Determination is unresolved. Probability is a candidate mathematical regime for uncertainty, not the definition of Knowledge. KnowledgeOS and Kernel architecture must remain downstream of these questions.
rows.statement: Freezes the current research boundary with eight explicit status declarations: Knowledge is not yet formally defined; Knowledge Space is not yet formally defined; Ideal State is not yet formally defined; Dimension is a working concept; Observation is a working concept; Determination is unresolved; Probability is a candidate mathematical regime for uncertainty, not the definition of Knowledge; KnowledgeOS and Kernel architecture must remain downstream of all these questions.
invariants: KnowledgeOS/Kernel architecture decisions must remain downstream of the unresolved ontology questions

rows.anchor: We have gone from: "What should the Kernel contain?" to a more fundamental investigation: What must be true about an epistemic determination for us to call it Knowledge? We should not answer this ourselves yet. This is the point to return to epistemology sources -- especially Pritchard's What Is This Thing Called Knowledge? ... The purpose is to challenge our model, not to force philosophy into KnowledgeOS.
rows.statement: Sets the next research phase: having moved from 'what should the Kernel contain?' to the more fundamental 'what must be true about an epistemic determination for us to call it Knowledge?', explicitly declines to answer this internally and instead plans to return to epistemology sources -- especially Pritchard's 'What Is This Thing Called Knowledge?' -- comparing the emerging model against established theories of Knowledge, Justification, Truth, Evidence, Belief, Fallibilism, and Epistemic luck; the stated purpose is to challenge the model, not to force philosophy into KnowledgeOS.
invariants: philosophy is consulted to challenge the model, never imported wholesale as KnowledgeOS architecture

rows.anchor: Knowledge can increase while the existing determination remains unchanged. So: Delta-Knowledge != Delta-Determination. A new fact can enrich KnowledgeOS without changing the business conclusion. ... KnowledgeOS does not have to decide. It can present: evidence A; evidence B; ... The owner decides. So: Knowledge -> Determinations -> Human/Business Decision but KnowledgeOS should not arbitrarily collapse conflicting knowledge.
rows.statement: Two further distinctions: (1) Knowledge and Determination are different -- Knowledge can increase while an existing determination stays unchanged (Delta-Knowledge != Delta-Determination), e.g. a new fact enriching KnowledgeOS without changing the business conclusion; (2) Knowledge and Decision are different -- KnowledgeOS presents evidence/reasoning/conflicts/relevant dimensions rather than deciding, following Knowledge -> Determinations -> Human/Business Decision, and must not arbitrarily collapse conflicting knowledge into a single answer merely because a decision is required.
invariants: Knowledge, Determination, and Decision are three distinct things, never collapsed
KnowledgeOS never manufactures a single answer merely because a decision is required

rows.anchor: If security says: non-compliant and architecture says: compliant, KnowledgeOS should preserve both and warn the owner. It should not manufacture a single answer merely because a decision is required. ... Threat may determine priority: Threat -> Priority but priority belongs to the decision/investigation context, not to the definition of Knowledge itself. A dimension that is unimportant for today's decision is still part of the knowledge space.
rows.statement: Two further principles: (1) conflict itself is knowledge -- if security says 'non-compliant' and architecture says 'compliant', KnowledgeOS should preserve both and warn the owner rather than manufacture a single answer; (2) priority is not Knowledge -- Threat -> Priority belongs to the decision/investigation context, not to the definition of Knowledge itself, and a dimension unimportant for today's decision remains part of the knowledge space.
invariants: conflicting knowledge is preserved and surfaced, never silently resolved
priority/relevance-to-today's-decision is never confused with membership in the knowledge space

rows.anchor: Knowledge itself is not probability. Probability may be needed because: values can be uncertain; observations are incomplete; dimensions can be undiscovered; evidence can be incomplete; extraction from observations is uncertain. So: Knowledge != Probability but: Probability may be a regime for representing epistemic uncertainty. That is a much safer position.
rows.statement: Restates Knowledge != Probability, listing five reasons probability may still be needed (uncertain values, incomplete observations, undiscovered dimensions, incomplete evidence, uncertain extraction from observations); probability is a regime for representing epistemic uncertainty, not the definition of Knowledge -- called a much safer position than earlier framings.

rows.anchor: We have sufficient knowledge for the security decision, but we do not have complete knowledge of the Nexus state ... knowlege actually does not care if they are important or not. ... Knowledge != Decision Sufficiency and: Priority not-in Knowledge itself. Priority tells us what we need to investigate first, not what counts as Knowledge. ... Knowledge Space K_t vs Decision Space K_t^decision subset K_t. ... Threat -> Investigation Priority, not Threat -> Knowledge.
rows.statement: Formalizes the Knowledge/Decision-Sufficiency separation in depth: having information on only the few dimensions relevant to today's decision is 'sufficient knowledge for the security decision' but not 'complete knowledge of Nexus' -- these are different claims, since Knowledge does not care whether a dimension is important for the current decision (importance is a property of the decision, not of Knowledge). Formally, Knowledge != Decision Sufficiency and Priority is not in Knowledge itself -- priority tells us what to investigate first, not what counts as Knowledge. Separates Knowledge Space K_t from Decision Space K_t^decision subset-of K_t (varying per decision type -- security/architecture/migration have different-sized relevant subsets). Threat determines Investigation Priority, not Knowledge itself (Threat -> Investigation Priority, never Threat -> Knowledge).
invariants: Priority is never a member of the definition of Knowledge
Knowledge Completeness and Decision Sufficiency are measured separately, never conflated
Threat determines investigation priority, never Knowledge content itself

rows.anchor: Delta Knowledge != Delta Determination ... Knowledge increased. The compliance determination remains unchanged. ... Knowledge | Determination | Meaning: up/unchanged = more knowledge same conclusion; up/changed = more knowledge changes conclusion; up/strengthened; up/weakened; up/conflicted. ... Knowledge -> Determinations -> Human/Business Decision ... the relationship is not necessarily deterministic. Multiple determinations may exist: K -> {D_1,...,D_n}.
rows.statement: Formalizes Delta-Knowledge != Delta-Determination with a worked example (discovering fully-encrypted backup increases knowledge without changing the existing compliance determination), and tabulates five knowledge/determination transition types: knowledge up + determination unchanged (more knowledge, same conclusion), up+changed (conclusion changes), up+strengthened, up+weakened, up+conflicted (unresolved contradiction). Reaffirms Knowledge -> Determinations -> Human/Business Decision as non-deterministic: a single knowledge state can support multiple determinations K -> {D_1,...,D_n}, with the decision-maker choosing among them; KnowledgeOS is not primarily producing decisions but maintaining an evolving understanding, with decisions as a downstream consumer.
invariants: a change in Knowledge and a change in Determination are two independently-varying things

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS should preserve epistemic plurality rather than prematurely collapse it into a single answer. ... "Compliance = disputed; two justified determinations currently exist" ... it should not necessarily say: "I have decided which one is correct." That remains a human/governance responsibility unless an explicit rule gives the system authority to resolve that particular conflict.
rows.statement: States the candidate property 'KnowledgeOS should preserve epistemic plurality rather than prematurely collapse it into a single answer', requiring the Kernel to potentially represent multiple observations, sources, interpretations, justified determinations, contradictions, temporal validity, and relationships between determinations; when Security and Architecture evidence conflict, KnowledgeOS should record 'Compliance = disputed; two justified determinations currently exist' (preferred over silently picking one), and should say what it knows, what supports each side, that they conflict, and that owner attention is required -- but should not say 'I have decided which one is correct' unless an explicit rule grants it that authority. Candidate research result, not yet a Kernel requirement.
invariants: KnowledgeOS never silently resolves a conflict it has no explicit authority to resolve

rows.anchor: [0,1]\text{ is a value space, not yet a semantics.}
rows.statement: A value v=0.85 attached to a proposition could mean at least four different things: (A) P(p|E) probability the proposition is true; (B) Conf(F) confidence in the determination; (C) Strength(E,F) strength of evidence; (D) T(p) degree of truth. These share the interval [0,1] but are not mathematically interchangeable, so 'facts have probability' is unsafe; the safer claim is 'a fact/proposition may have a probabilistic epistemic assessment under a probabilistic regime' — [0,1] is a value space, not yet a semantics.

rows.anchor: Reasoning = Premises + Inference Rules
rows.statement: Separates Logical entailment (A,A->B ⊢ B) from Uncertainty propagation (P(A)=0.8 does not by logic alone give P(B)=0.8 without a probabilistic model) as two distinct structures. Corrects 'Reason=Logic' to Reasoning=Premises+Inference Rules, since premises (A, A->B) themselves come from observations, prior facts, documented rules, principles, laws, methods, or institutional decisions.

rows.anchor: K_t^* \text{ contains the best justified epistemic state for every relevant question at }t.
rows.statement: Questions whether the ideal Knowledge state K_t* assigns every proposition value in {0,1}, or whether some questions (e.g. 'will event X happen tomorrow?') are fundamentally indeterminate even ideally. Proposes redefining K_t* as containing 'the best justified epistemic state for every relevant question at t' rather than requiring binary truth values, so V_t(p)=0.8 could be the CORRECT ideal state rather than an imperfect approximation — distinguishing Incomplete Knowledge (V̂_t(p)=0.7 while V_t*(p)=1) from Irreducible uncertainty (V_t*(p)=0.7 itself), called 'one of the most important problems we have uncovered'.
missing: formal resolution of whether K_t* permits non-binary values

rows.statement: States four nested research problems: (A) Determination — how do evidence+premises+logic produce a determined proposition?; (B) Epistemic value — what does v∈[0,1] mean when determination is not binary?; (C) Ideal state — what is K_t* and does it contain irreducible uncertainty or only incomplete knowledge?; (D) Reconstruction — what history must be preserved to reconstruct why F was determined? (flagged as leading toward the Kernel). Central invariant chain: PROPOSITION ≠ REASONING ≠ DETERMINATION ≠ EPISTEMIC VALUE ≠ KNOWLEDGE STATE, with p (proposition), R(p) (reasoning), D(p,R) (determination), V_t(p) (epistemic assessment), K_t={p_i,R_i,D_i,V_i,...} (candidate Knowledge state representation, explicitly marked 'candidate' pending lens-testing).
invariants: PROPOSITION ≠ REASONING ≠ DETERMINATION ≠ EPISTEMIC VALUE ≠ KNOWLEDGE STATE

rows.anchor: classical logic → probabilistic inference → evidence theory → fuzzy/many-valued logic → temporal logic → epistemic logic → argumentation → Nyāya → Navya-Nyāya → DDD → measurement theory → information theory → causal reasoning.
rows.statement: Recommends halting Kernel definition and instead running a cross-lens experiment: trace one concrete proposition (e.g. an election example) through Observation->Evidence->Premises->Logic->Determination->Value->Knowledge, then re-analyze the same episode through twelve lenses (classical logic, probabilistic inference, evidence theory, fuzzy/many-valued logic, temporal logic, epistemic logic, argumentation, Nyāya, Navya-Nyāya, DDD, measurement theory, information theory, causal reasoning). The key question is not which lens wins but 'what structure is present in every valid interpretation?' — that surviving structure is the strongest candidate for the true KnowledgeOS substrate.

rows.anchor: extraction-retrieves-material-determination-establishes-warrant -- second turning point -- extraction != determination ... kernel-problem-minimum-substrate-for-conditional-determination and determination-is-the-missing-mathematical-object -- third turning point -- Determination named as the missing object
rows.statement: Restates, from save-order timeline evidence, R1's second and third turning points: 'extraction retrieves material; determination establishes warrant' (extraction != determination), and shortly after, 'Determination is the missing mathematical object' -- matching the already-registered determination-as-mathematical-object concept, here dated to 2026-08-25 23:44-23:58 and framed as the pivotal derivation closing R1.

lineage_claims.quote: Determination is the missing mathematical object

rows.anchor: C-001 Knowledge is probably not the Kernel object ... HYPOTHESIS OPEN | C-002 Extraction retrieves material; determination establishes what it warrants asserting ... DERIVED OPEN | C-003 Determination is the missing mathematical object of the framework ... HYPOTHESIS
rows.statement: Registers claims C-001 (Knowledge probably not the Kernel object, HYPOTHESIS/OPEN), C-002 (extraction != determination, DERIVED/OPEN) and C-003 (Determination is the missing mathematical object, HYPOTHESIS, only partially formalized via R5 step-008 acceptance/commitment, with no computational test or repository validation established).

operational.anchor: I would not add another 20 concepts to KnowledgeOS. Instead, I would test our theory with real cases. Take three radically different cases: Case 1 -- Descriptive ... Case 2 -- Evaluative ... Case 3 -- Predictive ... If the same conceptual machinery works across them, we have evidence. If it doesn't, we have discovered that Knowledge is not one mechanism.

governance.anchor: Level 1 -- Business problem: How do we know what we currently know? Level 2 -- Scientific problem: How does incomplete, conditional and conflicting evidence become a justified determination? Level 3 -- KnowledgeOS problem: What minimum information must be preserved so that those determinations can be reconstructed, challenged and revised using different reasoning methods? And we are currently working on Level 2. We should not jump to Level 3 and define the Kernel yet.

rationale_evidence.anchor: certainty of the rule != certainty of its premises != certainty of the conclusion. This is precisely the combination problem that the framework identifies but hasn't yet solved.
rationale_evidence.statement: Challenges the framework's use of the word 'established' for facts feeding logic/rules: a fact can have a graded epistemic state (e.g. P(F1)=0.8) even while the logical rule F1 and F2 => K applying to it is completely valid; therefore certainty of the rule, certainty of its premises, and certainty of the conclusion are three distinct things -- this is the combination problem the framework identifies but has not yet solved.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Strong: correctly separates probability from Knowledge; correctly identifies conditional evidence; correctly identifies conditional reasoning; correctly keeps this as research rather than architecture; correctly demands cross-framework comparison. Needs correction: P(F|O) is too simplistic; "established facts" should not automatically be treated as deterministic; the listed common properties are not yet proven invariants; the common algebraic structure is premature; epistemic state may be multidimensional; determination is currently missing as an explicit mathematical object.
rationale_evidence.statement: Gives an explicit verdict on the uploaded framework document: five strong points (correctly separates probability from Knowledge; correctly identifies conditional evidence; correctly identifies conditional reasoning; correctly keeps this as research rather than architecture; correctly demands cross-framework comparison) and six points needing correction (P(F|O) too simplistic; 'established facts' should not automatically be treated as deterministic; listed common properties are not yet proven invariants; the common algebraic structure is premature; epistemic state may be multidimensional; determination is currently missing as an explicit mathematical object). Also explicitly agrees with the framework's constraint: 'Do not design the Kernel. Do not change its boundary. Challenge the architecture; do not become its architect.'

rationale_evidence.anchor: Port 8081 is open. That's an observation. Does it prove Nexus is available? No. It is evidence supporting that possibility. ... another process uses the port; the service is running but inaccessible from the required network; the information is outdated; this is not the production server. So: Observation != Evidence != Fact.
rationale_evidence.statement: Problem 1 (Information is not automatically evidence): 'Port 8081 is open' is an observation, not proof that Nexus is available -- it is evidence supporting that possibility only, since alternative explanations exist (another process on the port, network-inaccessible service, outdated information, wrong server); therefore Observation != Evidence != Fact.

rationale_evidence.anchor: A system is "migration ready" only if: dependencies are identified; network access is verified; backup is verified; certificates are understood; rollback is defined. ... Dependencies: Strong, Network: Strong, Backup: Uncertain, Certificates: Missing, Rollback: Strong. Can we say "Migration ready"? Not simply by looking at the data. We need the rule for determining readiness.
rationale_evidence.statement: Problem 3 (the rules for determining something matter): given a five-criterion migration-readiness policy (dependencies/network/backup/certificates/rollback) and mixed evidence strength per criterion (Strong/Strong/Uncertain/Missing/Strong), whether 'migration ready' can be asserted cannot be read off the data alone -- an explicit rule for determining readiness is required.

rationale_evidence.anchor: We have solved a substantial part of the conceptual problem, but we have not yet solved the formal definition of Knowledge or the Kernel. ... I would say we have solved perhaps 60-70% of the conceptual framing, but only 20-30% of the formal problem.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Knowledge != probability: Strong. Information != knowledge: Strong. Knowledge changes with time: Strong. ... One universal ideal state: Not established. rationale_evidence.statement: Gives an 18-row status table rating each research claim from this thread: strongly established (Knowledge!=probability, Information!=knowledge, Knowledge changes with time, observation is context/comparison dependent, probability as an uncertainty regime, dimension uncertainty, value uncertainty, multiple kinds of knowledge), strong hypothesis (reference/ideal state is important), interesting-but-unproven or useful-but-undefined (knowledge as subset of ideal state, infinite Knowledge Space, determination, fact-as-determination), and not established/rejected/unresolved (one universal ideal state, probability as universal extraction mechanism, epistemic equivalence, minimum substrate, KnowledgeOS Kernel -- explicitly 'not ready to define').

rationale_evidence.anchor: What is the State? -> What are its Dimensions? -> Which Dimensions are Relevant? -> What are their Ideal/Reference Values? -> What can be Observed? -> How is Information Extracted? -> How is Evidence evaluated? -> How is Reasoning performed? -> How is a Determination established? -> When does Determination become Knowledge? -> How is Knowledge revised over Time? -> What must be preserved? -> What is Kernel-essential? ... rationale_evidence.statement: Represents the whole research problem as a 13-step chain: State -> Dimensions -> Relevant Dimensions -> Ideal/Reference Values -> Observable -> Information Extraction -> Evidence Evaluation -> Reasoning -> Determination -> Determination-becomes-Knowledge -> Revision over Time -> What must be preserved -> Kernel-essential; self-assesses that meaningful progress has been made through roughly the middle of the chain, with the bottom half (determination onward) still unresolved.

rationale_evidence.anchor: If security says: non-compliant and architecture says: compliant, KnowledgeOS should preserve both and warn the owner. It should not manufacture a single answer merely because a decision is required. ... Threat may determine priority: Threat -> Priority but priority belongs to the decision/investigation context, not to the definition of Knowledge itself. A dimension that is unimportant for today's decision is still part of the knowledge space.
rationale_evidence.statement: Two further principles: (1) conflict itself is knowledge -- if security says 'non-compliant' and architecture says 'compliant', KnowledgeOS should preserve both and warn the owner rather than manufacture a single answer; (2) priority is not Knowledge -- Threat -> Priority belongs to the decision/investigation context, not to the definition of Knowledge itself, and a dimension unimportant for today's decision remains part of the knowledge space.

rationale_evidence.anchor: [0,1]\text{ is a value space, not yet a semantics.}
rationale_evidence.statement: A value v=0.85 attached to a proposition could mean at least four different things: (A) P(p|E) probability the proposition is true; (B) Conf(F) confidence in the determination; (C) Strength(E,F) strength of evidence; (D) T(p) degree of truth. These share the interval [0,1] but are not mathematically interchangeable, so 'facts have probability' is unsafe; the safer claim is 'a fact/proposition may have a probabilistic epistemic assessment under a probabilistic regime' — [0,1] is a value space, not yet a semantics.
