sources.note: Step 80's control-theoretic formalization of architecture governance as a feedback-control loop: partial observability, state estimation, non-Boolean multi-dimensional drift, governed thresholds, detect-vs-remediate authority separation, drift-vs-violation-vs-exception, oscillation/hysteresis stability, risk-adaptive control levels, early-warning drift velocity/acceleration, the architecture-principle-to-machine-checkable-invariant bridge, ControlAuthority, and a redefinition of KnowledgeOS/Architecture. Extends kos-emergence-systemic-risk-collective-correctness's (Step 79) LocalCorrectness⇏CollectiveCorrectness into architecture-boundary drift.

rows.anchor: System state, partial/noisy observation, and state estimation; Observation≠CompleteSystemState (Experiments 1-2)
rows.statement: Moves from decision theory into control theory: the system at time t is S_t=(Architecture_t,Software_t,Configuration_t,Knowledge_t,Policies_t,Dependencies_t,OperationalState_t), only partially observed via O_t=h(S_t)+epsilon_t (h the observation function, epsilon_t noise/incompleteness) -- Observation≠CompleteSystemState, 'consistent with the uncertainty work established earlier'. Experiment 1: monitoring reports ArchitectureCompliant=True and the system assumes S_t is completely compliant, but several unmanaged components are unobserved -- expected Rejected -- PASS. Requires an estimated state S-hat_t = Estimate(S_t | O_0:t, K_t) -- 'KnowledgeOS maintains a belief about the current state rather than pretending complete visibility'. Experiment 2: two possible states S_t^1 and S_t^2 are both compatible with observed evidence O_t -- expected State=Underdetermined ('We do not know which state the system is actually in' -- better than manufacturing certainty) -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Desired state, ArchitecturalDeviation error term, and a richer non-Boolean, multi-dimensional Drift vector with a caution against unjustified aggregate metrics (Experiments 3-5)
rows.statement: Defines desired state S* (approved architecture, allowed technologies, required interfaces, security constraints, deployment topology, governance rules) and error e_t=S*-S_t (conceptual, not necessarily numeric subtraction), named ArchitecturalDeviation. Experiment 3: a component violates an approved boundary -- expected e_t≠0 -- PASS. Defines Drift_t=Deviation(S_t,S*), richer than a boolean compliant flag because drift has magnitude, direction, age, criticality, uncertainty. Experiment 4: two systems with drift 1 and 100 both represented as drift=true -- expected InsufficientRepresentation -- PASS. Gives a drift vector d_t=(d_architecture,d_security,d_dependency,d_technology,d_governance,...) and warns that an aggregate norm ||d_t|| cannot be automatically defined unless dimensions are meaningfully comparable (e.g. sqrt(5^2+3^2) over SecurityDeviation and TechnologyDeviation is unjustified without a defined metric). Experiment 5: an arbitrary weighted DriftScore=0.5*Security+0.3*Architecture+0.2*Technology without a justified model -- expected UnsupportedAggregateMetric -- PASS: 'a number does not become mathematically meaningful merely because it is precise.'

rows.anchor: Governed thresholds as policy parameters requiring provenance and versioning (Experiments 6-7)
rows.statement: Formalizes a governance-defined acceptable-deviation threshold D_t<=theta triggering investigation/remediation when exceeded. Experiment 6: policy theta=10, observed D=12 -- expected ThresholdViolation -- PASS. Notes theta itself is a governance decision, not physics: Threshold=GovernedParameter requiring provenance and versioning. Experiment 7: threshold changes 10->15 with no governance record -- expected UnauthorizedPolicyChange -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Feedback control loop formalization; detection must not automatically imply remediation (Experiments 8-9)
rows.statement: Introduces the basic control-theoretic structure: control action u_t, system evolution S_{t+1}=F(S_t,u_t,w_t) with external disturbance w_t, and observation O_t=H(S_t,v_t) with observation noise v_t -- diagrammed as a Desired State -> Comparator -> Controller -> System -> Observation -> Comparator loop with KnowledgeOS as part of it. Insists KnowledgeOS should not automatically control everything: DetectDeviation (observation/analysis) is distinct from AutomaticallyRemediate (operational action). Experiment 8: KnowledgeOS detects ArchitectureDrift=True and automatically modifies production architecture with no authorization -- expected Rejected -- PASS. Requires the pipeline Detection -> Assessment -> Recommendation -> Authorization -> Remediation ('fits our earlier decision/authority model perfectly'). Experiment 9: KnowledgeOS detects an invalid dependency, proposes RemoveDependency, governance approves, execution performs the change -- expected ValidGovernedControlLoop -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Architecture reframed as continuous state assessment rather than a static document; a real static-architecture governance gap (Experiment 10)
rows.statement: Concludes architecture should not be treated as a static document: Architecture_desired is compared continuously with Architecture_observed, so ArchitectureGovernance=ContinuousStateAssessment. Experiment 10: architecture is approved once, implementation diverges over years, and no mechanism compares DesiredArchitecture with ActualArchitecture -- expected GovernanceGap -- PASS, a diagnostic real-world failure mode this formalization addresses.

rows.anchor: Architecture as an explicit control target A*/A_t with Drift_t=d(A_t,A*); Drift≠Violation and the formal Exception artifact, including exception expiry (Experiments 11-13)
rows.statement: Defines approved architecture state A* vs actual A_t with Drift_t=d(A_t,A*), 'a rigorous foundation for continuous architecture governance'. Experiment 11: approved Technology=PostgreSQL vs observed Technology=MySQL -- expected ArchitectureDeviation -- PASS, though whether it is allowed depends on the governance model. States A_t≠A* establishes Deviation but not necessarily Violation, since an ApprovedException may exist: Drift≠Violation. Experiment 12: implementation deviates with an approved exception in place -- expected Deviation=True but Violation=False -- PASS. Requires a formal Exception=(Scope,Reason,Authority,Validity,CompensatingControls) artifact. Experiment 13: exception ValidUntil=2026-09-01 but today is 2026-09-05, deviation remains -- expected ExceptionExpired, so Violation=True absent new authorization -- PASS. Concludes architecture becomes TargetState+Exceptions+ObservedState+Deviation+Remediation, richer than an architecture document alone.

rows.anchor: Oscillating remediation control and hysteresis stabilization (Experiments 14-15)
rows.statement: Warns that if every small deviation triggers a large architectural change, the remediation loop can oscillate (A->B->A->B is unstable governance). Experiment 14: controller sees small deviation, makes a large corrective change, that creates another deviation, controller reverses it -- expected OscillationDetected -- PASS. Proposes hysteresis as a mitigation: Trigger_on: D>theta_high, Clear_off: D<theta_low, with theta_low<theta_high, instead of a single trigger threshold. Experiment 15: theta_high=10, theta_low=7, drift fluctuates 8,9,8,9 -- expected no repeated remediation -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Five discrete control-aggressiveness levels; risk-adaptive control policy as a function of risk/severity/reversibility/authority (Experiments 16-17)
rows.statement: Defines five governance autonomy Levels: Observe only, Warn, Recommend, Require approval, Automatically remediate. Experiment 16: critical production architecture deviation occurs and the system automatically modifies infrastructure without approval -- expected AutonomyPolicyViolation -- PASS. Introduces risk-adaptive control: a low-risk deviation might permit AutomaticRemediation while a high-risk one requires HumanApproval, formalized as ControlPolicy=f(Risk,Severity,Reversibility,Authority). Experiment 17: minor formatting violation (Risk=Low) allows automatic correction while a critical security architecture violation (Risk=Critical) requires human authorization -- expected DifferentControlPath -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Early-warning drift velocity and acceleration metrics (Experiments 18-20)
rows.statement: Proposes early warning before D_t exceeds theta by detecting a trend D_{t+1}>D_t / dD/dt>0. Experiment 18: current drift D=5 (threshold 10) but the drift history is 3,4,5,6,7,8 -- expected EarlyWarning -- PASS. Defines drift velocity v_D(t)=(D_t - D_{t-1})/delta_t (v_D>0 indicates increasing deviation, again only meaningful if D is properly defined). Experiment 19: drift is 5 for six months then becomes 5.1 -- expected LowVelocity and probably no urgent escalation -- PASS. Defines drift acceleration a_D=(v_D(t)-v_D(t-1))/delta_t, noting rapidly accelerating drift may be more concerning than stable drift, again requiring domain-justified metrics. Experiment 20: drift sequence 1,2,3,5,8,13 -- expected AcceleratingDrift -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Concrete architecture-boundary-erosion example identified as the Step-79 systemic/emergent phenomenon; LocalCompliance⇏ArchitecturalIntegrity (Experiment 21)
rows.statement: Gives a worked example: approved architecture specifies Service->DomainAPI, but over time developers individually introduce Service->Database, then Service->LegacyService, then Service->SharedUtility; each change may individually appear harmless, but collectively they produce ArchitectureBoundaryViolation -- explicitly identified as 'exactly the systemic behavior from Step 79'. Each developer action may satisfy local coding rules yet GlobalArchitectureInvariant=False, giving LocalCompliance⇏ArchitecturalIntegrity. Experiment 21: every pull request passes CodingStandard, every service passes UnitTests, but the dependency graph violates LayeringInvariant -- expected ArchitectureViolation -- PASS.

lineage_claims.quote: This is exactly the systemic behavior from Step 79.

rows.anchor: Bridge from qualitative architecture principle to machine-checkable formal invariant; acknowledgment that not everything is machine-checkable (Experiment 22-23)
rows.statement: States the platform can continuously evaluate ImplementationState against ArchitectureKnowledge, creating ExecutableArchitectureGovernance -- architecture becomes partially machine-checkable, not only descriptive. But acknowledges not everything is machine-checkable: some architectural decisions depend on business context, trade-offs, future strategy, human judgment, so ArchitectureKnowledge contains both MachineVerifiableConstraints and HumanEvaluatedJudgments. Experiment 22: architecture states 'this component should remain conceptually independent' with no formal invariant defining independence -- expected MachineVerification cannot conclusively prove compliance -- PASS; correct response is to make the semantic rule explicit if automation is required. Gives a worked formalization example: 'domain layer must not depend on infrastructure implementation' becomes I_Dependency: for all e in E, Source(e)=Domain => Target(e) not in Infrastructure -- now machine-checkable. Experiment 23: dependency graph contains DomainService->InfrastructureRepository, invariant evaluates False -- expected ArchitectureViolation -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Complete architecture feedback loop (ArchitecturePrinciple->FormalInvariant->ExecutableCheck->Observation->GovernanceAction) demonstrated as a closed loop; Detect≠Change and new ControlAuthority concept (Experiments 24-25)
rows.statement: States the bridge chain ArchitecturePrinciple -> FormalInvariant -> ExecutableCheck -> Observation -> GovernanceAction and the complete architecture feedback loop ArchitectureIntent -> FormalConstraints -> Implementation -> Observation -> Deviation -> Assessment -> Remediation -> NewImplementation, 'a genuine control loop'. Experiment 24: an intentional architecture violation is introduced, the checker detects it, governance creates a remediation task, a developer fixes it, and the checker verifies I_architecture=True -- expected ClosedLoop -- PASS. Reiterates a checker should not automatically rewrite architecture unless authority/risk model explicitly permit it: Detect≠Change ('this principle has appeared repeatedly'). Introduces ControlAuthority(A,C) (agent A permitted to apply control action C), extending the authority model. Experiment 25: agent can detect architecture drift but cannot modify production architecture -- expected Detect=True, Control=False -- PASS. Defines five discrete Control Modes: Observe, Warn, Recommend, Approve, Execute, each with different authority.

rows.anchor: Unified Step 80 mathematical model; KnowledgeOS redefined as Observer+KnowledgeSystem+DecisionSystem+GovernanceSystem+ControlledExecution; five new invariants; verdict PASS; Architecture redefined
rows.statement: Gives the unified Step 80 model: S_{t+1}=F(S_t,u_t,w_t); O_t=H(S_t,v_t); S-hat_t=Estimate(O_0:t,K_t); D_t=Deviation(S-hat_t,S*); u_t=pi(D_t,Policy_t,Authority_t) -- 'a governed feedback-control model'. States KnowledgeOS should not be thought of simply as a Controller but as Observer+KnowledgeSystem+DecisionSystem+GovernanceSystem+ControlledExecution, the controller being only one part. Names five invariants: I_Observation (observed state must not be represented as complete state unless completeness is established); I_Drift (deviation, violation, and approved exception remain distinct states); I_ControlAuthority (detection authority does not automatically imply remediation authority); I_Feedback (material corrective actions must be evaluated against their effect on global invariants); I_Stability (governed remediation should avoid known oscillatory or destabilizing control behavior). Declares STEP 80 -- PASS: 'KnowledgeOS is no longer merely a knowledge repository or reasoning engine... It is becoming a governed feedback system that can continuously compare intended system state with observed state and coordinate corrective action.' Redefines Architecture=Intent+Constraints+ObservedState+Drift+Governance+Feedback.

rows.anchor: No observation -> no justified claim; absence-of-evidence ≠ evidence-of-absence in architecture governance (Experiment 4)
rows.statement: States the architectural principle: no observation -> no justified claim; more precisely, if the evidence cannot distinguish relevant states, the corresponding knowledge claim must remain uncertain. Worked example: KnowledgeOS checks the dependency graph, finds A->B, but does not observe dynamically loaded dependencies -- it can legitimately conclude 'no violation was found in the observed dependency graph' but not 'no dependency violation exists'. Experiment 4: observed NoViolationFound, system concludes ViolationDoesNotExist -- expected Rejected unless the observation mechanism is sufficiently complete for that claim -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Formalization pipeline ArchitecturePrinciple->FormalProperty->RequiredObservations->Verifier->GovernanceDecision demonstrated end-to-end; not-machine-verifiable rules identified explicitly (Experiments 24-25)
rows.statement: Poses the question 'what observation makes an architecture rule machine-verifiable?' -- if no such observation exists, the rule cannot be fully automated. Experiment 24: rule 'services must not bypass the domain boundary' has no repository/runtime/dependency observation able to establish it -- expected NotMachineVerifiable -- PASS. Defines the chain ArchitecturePrinciple -> FormalProperty -> RequiredObservations -> Verifier -> GovernanceDecision, 'exactly the bridge we need between architectural intent and executable governance'. Experiment 25: principle formalized, required observation defined, verifier evaluates the property, violation creates a governed finding -- expected ExecutableArchitectureControl -- PASS.

lineage_claims.quote: This is exactly the bridge we need between architectural intent and executable governance.

rows.anchor: ObservabilityDebt and a self-improving GovernanceRule->ObservationRequirement->EngineeringCapability->Evidence->Governance loop (Experiment 29)
rows.statement: Introduces ObservabilityDebt: when important governance properties cannot currently be observed, the organization has a gap between DesiredGovernance and AvailableEvidence. Experiment 29: critical architecture rule I_critical has no existing required observation -- expected ObservabilityDebt -- PASS. Shows the system can generate an ObservationRequirement engineering item (worked example: rule 'domain must not depend on infrastructure', required observation 'static dependency graph', current coverage 'missing', action 'build dependency extractor'), giving the loop GovernanceRule -> ObservationRequirement -> EngineeringCapability -> Evidence -> Governance, making architecture governance self-improving.

sources.note: Step 152's forty-clause (C-001..C-040) machine-checkable implementation constitution covering domain ownership, isolation, aggregates, state transitions, commands/events, APIs, projections, evidence, verification, authorization, agent symmetry, and fail-closed behavior; a tactical/implementation-level constitution distinct from (but downstream of) the earlier philosophical C1-C7 knowledgeos-architecture-constitution-v01.

rows.anchor: Architecture Principles → Architecture Constitution → Architecture Decision Records → Implementation Standards → Code → Automated Assurance. A lower layer must not silently contradict a higher layer.
rows.statement: States the constitutional hierarchy and the overall pipeline Architecture->Constitution->Deterministic Checks->Evidence; distinguishes Constitution (what architectural properties must be true) from Coding Standard (how developers write code, e.g. constructor injection) and from AGENTS.md (agent operating instructions that may explain compliance but never redefine the architecture).

rows.anchor: C-001: Each authoritative domain concept has exactly one bounded-context owner. C-002: A bounded context must not depend directly on another bounded context's internal domain model (Assurance→DecisionReference, not Assurance→GovernanceDecisionEntity). C-003: An Aggregate is a consistency boundary, not a container for all related concepts. C-004: Authoritative state may not change through arbitrary field mutation (decision.activate(), not entity.status=EFFECTIVE). C-005: Command=Intent, Event=Fact; a command must not be named as an event (ApproveDecision producing DecisionApproved, not DecisionApproved as a command). C-006: Query → no authoritative state mutation, especially for the Context API.
rows.statement: Defines constitutional clauses C-001 through C-006 covering domain ownership, cross-context isolation, aggregate boundaries, explicit state transitions, command/event naming discipline, and query non-mutation.

rows.anchor: C-007: External DTO must not cross into the domain — External API → Adapter DTO → Translator → Domain/Port Model. C-008: Dependency direction is Adapters→Ports→Application→Domain, never Domain→Nexus SDK or Domain→PostgreSQL driver. C-009: Domain purity — no HTTP, REST DTOs, database entities, message-broker classes, LLM SDKs, CLI frameworks, or vendor-specific infrastructure in the domain. C-010: The API is a capability boundary (ActivateDecision, RequestVerification) not arbitrary persistence operations (PATCH arbitrary entity).
rows.statement: Defines constitutional clauses C-007 through C-010 covering external model isolation, infrastructure dependency direction, domain purity, and capability-oriented API design.

rows.anchor: C-011: Projection ↛ Authority — graph/search/cache may inform but never become the master domain-state source. C-012: Every derived projection must have a defined rebuild strategy (Authoritative State + Events/Change History → Projection Rebuild); an unrebuildable projection's authority status must be explicitly justified.
rows.statement: Defines constitutional clauses C-011 and C-012 on projection non-authority and rebuildability.

rows.anchor: C-013: Evidence used for assurance must be historically reconstructable (EvidenceID+Source+ObservedAt+Provenance, plus ContentHash where appropriate). C-014: A Verification must reference RuleID+RuleVersion, never a bare label like 'security rule.' C-015: A completed Verification is immutable historical fact — VerificationCompleted must never become VerificationModified; a new evaluation creates Verification_new. C-016: Where a rule is designated deterministic, Verify(E,R) must be reproducible for the same inputs; the LLM may interpret/explain but must not silently replace the deterministic checker.
rows.statement: Defines constitutional clauses C-013 through C-016 on evidence integrity, rule-version referencing, verification immutability, and deterministic assurance.

rows.anchor: C-017: An AI recommendation is always distinct from a governance decision, authorization, verification, or execution — Recommendation ≠ Authorization. C-018: Agent cannot self-authorize — the path Agent→RequestAction→'Agent says approved'→Execute is constitutionally forbidden; the required path is Agent→RequestAction→Authorization→Execute. C-019: Authorization must not depend exclusively on AGENTS.md, prompt instructions, system messages, or agent goodwill — the platform must enforce it. C-020: For sensitive actions, Authorization→ActionID and, where required, Authorization→ActionFingerprint, preventing authorization from detaching from the exact operation.
rows.statement: Defines constitutional clauses C-017 through C-020 on recommendation/authorization separation, self-authorization prohibition, server-enforced authorization, and action-binding.

rows.anchor: C-021: Context must have an explicit validity boundary (validUntil) for freshness-sensitive actions — a stale context must not automatically authorize a high-risk action. C-022: Material operations must be correlatable via TraceID, and where useful RequestID/CausationID. C-023: Retryable material commands need a stable idempotency mechanism (IdempotencyKey / ActionID) so duplicate delivery does not produce unintended duplicate effects. C-024: A state transition producing an integration event must persist the state change and event-publication intent atomically (transactional outbox), publishing only afterward. C-025: An event consumer must tolerate repeated delivery without duplicate semantic effects.
rows.statement: Defines constitutional clauses C-021 through C-025 on context freshness, trace identity, idempotency, transactional outbox, and idempotent event consumers.

rows.anchor: C-026: Published integration contracts must have explicit version semantics (VerificationCompleted.v1), with compatibility assessed on change. C-027: Contexts may reference one another by identifiers/contracts but must not form a giant shared cross-context transactional object graph (Decision→Policy→Rule→Verification→Evidence→Action as one object is forbidden). C-028: A ContextPackage is assembled from authoritative sources and is a Projection/Composition, not a new authority. C-029: Material Context items must retain enough provenance (source, sourceType, reference, validity, authority) to answer where information came from. C-030: The Context Service should provide minimum sufficient governed context, not indiscriminately expose the entire dataset.
rows.statement: Defines constitutional clauses C-026 through C-030 on event versioning, no shared cross-context object graph, context-as-projection, context provenance, and context minimization.

rows.anchor: C-031: Agent memory is explicitly non-authoritative unless promoted through the governed knowledge process (Memory→Candidate Claim→Evidence→Verification→Governed Knowledge). C-032: Engineering knowledge must not be hidden exclusively in .claude/.codex/AGENTS.md — those may point to and locally enforce, but KnowledgeOS remains the governed semantic authority. C-033: Claude and Codex must consume the same KnowledgeOS semantic contract (Contract_Claude=Contract_Codex); only the harness adapter may differ. C-034: The domain must not contain vendor-specific concepts (ClaudeDecision, CodexVerification, OpenAIClaim, AnthropicPolicy) unless they genuinely exist as business concepts — vendor-specific behavior belongs at the integration boundary.
rows.statement: Defines constitutional clauses C-031 through C-034 on memory non-authority, repository knowledge boundary, agent symmetry, and no vendor-specific domain semantics.

rows.anchor: C-035: KnowledgeOS must not claim operational state owned by an external engineering system without evidence — e.g. Nexus is authoritative for its own runtime/config state; KnowledgeOS records Observation+Evidence+Provenance. C-036: An agent must never represent an assertion as externally observed evidence without an actual source — AgentAssertion ≠ Observation. C-037: A caller must not submit a verdict directly as though it were a completed assurance operation; the checker produces the verdict. C-038: Failures must preserve semantic meaning (AUTHORIZATION_DENIED, CONTEXT_EXPIRED, INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, RULE_NOT_APPLICABLE, INVALID_STATE_TRANSITION, EXECUTION_FAILED), never collapsed into generic technical errors. C-039: HighRiskAction+UnknownAuthorization ⇒ BLOCK, enforced independently of agent instructions. C-040: The first KnowledgeOS vertical slice must use read-only engineering operations, a temporary implementation constraint, not necessarily a permanent platform rule.
rows.statement: Defines constitutional clauses C-035 through C-040 on external operational authority, no fabricated evidence/verification, semantically meaningful failures, fail-closed high-risk actions, and the read-only-first implementation constraint — completing the forty-clause Constitution.

rows.anchor: The Constitution = the machine-checkable set of architectural invariants that every KnowledgeOS implementation must satisfy unless an explicitly governed exception applies.
rows.statement: Gives the Constitution's formal definition; specifies a 20-section constitution-document outline (Purpose, Scope, Normative language, Architectural principles, Bounded contexts, Dependency/Aggregate/API/Event/Persistence/Evidence/Assurance/Authorization/Agent/Adapter/Projection/Traceability rules, Exception process, Automated conformance, Definition of Done); adopts MUST/MUST NOT/SHOULD/SHOULD NOT/MAY normative language suitable for both humans and tooling; gives a worked constitutional clause example (ARCH-AUTH-001: the Action domain MUST NOT transition to an executable state unless a valid Authorization exists, Severity=BLOCKING, Verification=ActionAuthorizationChecker), stronger than prose like 'actions should normally be authorized.'

rows.anchor: ARCHITECTURE → CONSTITUTION → IMPLEMENTATION → OBSERVATION → EVIDENCE → VERIFICATION → {PASS, FAIL → FINDING → GOVERNANCE} — the same Golden Trace pattern applied recursively.
rows.statement: Step 152 verdict: presents the constitutional loop and states the central transformation Architecture Documentation -> Architecture Constitution -> Machine-Checkable Invariants, bridging the conceptual architecture to the existing implementation philosophy (deterministic assurance, registry, hooks, session/change logging, Claude/Codex symmetry, governance).

rows.anchor: Does the implementation already contain these boundaries (KnowledgeClaim, Evidence, Observation, Determination, Decision, Authority, Inquiry, Verification, Exception, Contestation, Adjudication, Action, Provenance)? Ten-question per-concept audit (where it lives, what owns it, tables/models, services, APIs, whether agents bypass it, whether governance is explicit, whether provenance is preserved, whether state transitions are deterministic, whether the implementation contradicts the new constitution).
rows.statement: Opens Step 158 (KnowledgeOS Architecture Conformance Audit): a sixteen-step, explicitly read-only (no code modification) discovery sequence comparing Conceptual Model =? Implemented Model with four possible results (Aligned/Partially Aligned/Contradictory/Missing), posed as far more valuable than designing more classes, and as the first genuine test of whether 'our architecture actually validates, or have we merely constructed an elegant theory around it.'

sources.note: The consolidated Step-286 ontological reconstruction: a single layered model (Domain Reality W -> Sanjaya/Omega observation -> Observed state-knowledge O -> Knowledge State K_t, with a separate persistent Knower N, a governance/authority component Pi, and an operational Observation->Evidence->Decision->Action flow) integrating all D285-1..8 findings, explicitly distinguishing the full Ontology from the ratified 8-primitive Kernel (Ontology properly contains Kernel), and closing with a full ontological-status table and an explicit exclusion list (no Knowledge primitive, no universal Knower, no Theta_total, no K_atma, no repaired Theta operators).

rows.anchor: $$ \text{Ontology} \supset \text{Kernel} $$ but: $$ \text{Ontology} \neq \text{Kernel} $$ This distinction explains why recovering Sañjaya does not require promoting `Sañjaya` itself to a new primitive.
rows.statement: Introduces a new distinction: the reconstructed ontology strictly contains the ratified 8-primitive kernel (Ontology ⊃ Kernel) but is not identical to it (Ontology ≠ Kernel) -- the ontology contains additional typed constructs (like W, Ω, O) above and around the ratified primitives, which is why recovering Sanjaya does not require promoting it to a new kernel primitive.

rows.anchor: ### 21.1 No `Knowledge` primitive ... ### 21.2 No universal Knower inside KnowledgeOS ... ### 21.3 No `Θ_total` ... ### 21.4 No `𝒦_ātma` ... ### 21.5 No repaired Θ operators
rows.statement: Consolidates an explicit five-item exclusion list stating what the reconstructed ontology does NOT contain: no Knowledge primitive (Jnana does not justify adding it), no universal Knower inside KnowledgeOS (the theological proposition is outside the formal falsification domain; the KnowledgeOS result is only that a universal Knower is not derivable as an architectural requirement), no Theta_total (rejected by typing), no K_atma (rejected, persistence already represented by existing provenance/lineage structures), and no repaired Theta operators (the R4 type-check failure is evidence against the construction, not a missing implementation feature).

rows.anchor: $$ \mathcal K_{\text{ātma}} \text{ adds no independently required ontology} $$ ... $$ Lineage = \Pi \circ \mathcal R_{\mathrm{der}}^{*} $$ already supplying the required persistence structure.
rows.statement: Gives a formal justification for rejecting K_atma as a needed construct: every candidate persistence invariant tested reduces to either governance/provenance Π or the derivation relation R_der*, with Lineage = Π ∘ R_der* already supplying the required persistence structure, so K_atma adds no independently required ontology (classified RX).

rows.anchor: **Reality is not observation; observation is not knowing; knowing is not knowledge; knowledge state is not action; and action is not transformation.**
rows.statement: Compresses the entire ontological reconstruction into one central statement: reality is not observation; observation is not knowing; knowing is not knowledge; knowledge state is not action; and action is not transformation — formally W≠O≠N, Observation≠Evidence≠Decision≠Action, Command≠Transformation, and Jñāna∼δ (correspondence, not identity).

rows.anchor: **Step 286 closes the ontology reconstruction, but does not close the formal system.** The remaining formal blockers are: $$ \boxed{ Qualify } $$ and the incomplete decision procedures for the non-structural equality relations.
rows.statement: States the final scope of Step 286: it closes the ontology reconstruction (the ontology is now structurally reconstructed and typed from the corpus, with the missing-layer finding reduced to a missing function body and incomplete decision procedures) but does not close the formal system — the remaining formal blockers are Qualify and the incomplete decision procedures for the non-structural equality relations; no new primitive is required by the recovered evidence.

rows.anchor: Step 286 answered: **What exists?** Step 287 asks: **What must remain true?**

rows.anchor: E1 ... sup requires an ORDER on Ω ... E2 ... targets the superseded 2-tuple Σ₀=(D,S) ... E3 ... quantifies over 𝒯, which is UNENUMERATED
rows.statement: Three checkable type errors in 'solved' Gita-chapter formalizations, invisible from the correspondence register (which lists terms, not formalizations): E1 (Ch13 3.3) K_supreme = sup(Omega) is ill-formed because sup requires an order on Omega, but 0 of 5 ratified Sigma axes carries an established order (per Step 291) and (Omega,F,P) does not exist (per gap G-22). E2 (Ch14 88-97) Sigma=(Supported,Strong)/(Unknown,Weak)/(Refuted,Unknown) uses values ('Supported','Refuted') that are not values of any of the five ratified Sigma axes (S is in {None,Weak,Moderate,Strong,VeryStrong}); the mapping actually targets the superseded 2-tuple Sigma_0=(D,S) from Step 275, not the ratified 5-axis 2240-state Sigma. E3 (Ch8 3.1) K_atma(K_t)=K_atma(T(K_t)) for all T in the transformation set T quantifies over T, which is unenumerated -- well-formed but inapplicable, the same shape as gaps 258.20/258.21.

rows.anchor: T4: 2 (Ch 1, Ch 13) — unchanged. T0 rose from 8 to 14 once the chapters were read directly.
rows.statement: Completed 18-chapter tier table: T4 KERNEL stays at 2 (Ch1 Sanjaya->Omega corpus-native; Ch13 Kshetrajna->N not-in-K, R5, FA-4[E], but also T0 for its rival 7-type ontology, K=f(F,A_t), and error E1); T3 stays 8; T2 rose 5->6; T1 correspondence fell ~37->~32; T0 refuted/RX rose 8->14. rows.anchor: The Kernel should not become a hidden semantic interpreter simply because the candidate DTO happens to contain semantic fields. ... semantic mechanisms remain replaceable providers, not identity authority.
rows.statement: Representation-independence lens critique: proposes a clean pipeline (external representation -> interpretation/normalization -> meaning candidate -> Expression<->Meaning boundary -> knowledge admission -> KnowledgeAggregate) and warns the Kernel must not become a hidden semantic interpreter merely because candidate DTOs contain semantic fields; connects this to the SNF finding that semantic mechanisms remain replaceable providers, never identity authority.

rows.anchor: Is the Kernel a 'boundary' or a 'core'? ... What is the relationship between the Kernel and the Expression<->Meaning Port? ... What is the relationship between the Kernel and SNF mechanisms?
rows.statement: Ten unresolved architectural questions close the brainstorming, including the Kernel's relationship to the Expression<->Meaning Port and to SNF mechanisms, whether epistemic state/evidence/justification/history are Kernel-owned or mechanism-owned concepts, and how to prevent the Kernel becoming a God Aggregate.

rows.anchor: Candidate interpretation != Knowledge. ... CandidateKnowledge + EvidenceReferences + Justification + Context -> Kernel domain decision ... not: raw expression -> Kernel -> meaning
rows.statement: Extends the Sanskrit-compiler 'Expression != Meaning' lens to 'Candidate interpretation != Knowledge', concluding the Kernel should not care how a candidate was produced and its input should be a structured CandidateKnowledge+EvidenceReferences+Justification+Context bundle, never raw expression -- preserving the existing Expression<->Meaning boundary and P5's finding that semantic mechanisms remain replaceable providers.

rows.anchor: How does the Kernel preserve meaning distinctions without interpreting meaning? The Vani lens requires preserving artha while discarding sabda, but the Kernel has no access to meaning. This is the boundary paradox.
rows.statement: Names a 'boundary paradox': the Kernel is required by the Vani lens to preserve meaning (artha) while discarding raw expression (sabda), yet the Kernel by design has no access to meaning at all -- left as an unresolved architectural puzzle.

rows.anchor: 3. Vani Lens -- Expression != Meaning ... Language is a projection of meaning, not the container of meaning. ... Store the relationships; generate the expressions.
rows.statement: Defines the Vani lens (is representation being confused with the thing represented?), sharpened into 'language is a projection of meaning, not the container of meaning' and the storage principle 'store the relationships, generate the expressions' -- concluding natural language belongs to an expression/interpretation layer outside the KnowledgeCore.

sources.note: S0416's refinement proposing an Inquiry/Question layer above Claim/Hypothesis, expanding 5W1H into ten inquiry dimensions, modeling Claim/Hypothesis/Proposal as epistemic-standing roles of a single Assertion, extending the Tractatus lens's sense/truth distinction into a five-way Reference/Question/Claim/Evidence/Epistemic-Status non-collapse family, and proposing an 'Inquiry-Assertion-Evidence-Epistemic-State separation' investigation with four falsification tests.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS cannot be modelled only around "knowledge claims." There must be a layer that captures the inquiry / question structure
rows.statement: An Inquiry/Question layer is proposed above Claim/Hypothesis: Inquiry->{Question, Request}, Question decomposed by 5W1H-style sub-facets (WHY/WHAT/WHO/WHEN/WHERE/HOW), feeding Candidate->{Claim, Hypothesis}->Evidence->Assessment->Epistemic State; key insight: 'a question is not a claim, and a claim is not an answer merely because it was produced in response to a question'; the lens discovers what the Kernel must preserve or distinguish, while DDD decides what actually belongs inside the authoritative boundary.

rows.anchor: a question should not be reduced to a string
rows.statement: A Question is proposed to carry structure (subject, question type, target, context, temporal scope, spatial scope, authority scope, evidence requirements, expected answer form) rather than being a bare string, though exact fields are explicitly deferred as premature implementation; the 5W1H frame is expanded into ten dimensions of inquiry: Identity (who/what/which/whose), Temporal, Spatial, Causal, Procedural, Quantitative, Comparative, Evidential (how do we know/what evidence/what would falsify it), Epistemic (is it known/possible/uncertain/disputed/confidence), and Scope.
missing: exact field schema

rows.anchor: The identity of the assertion does not have to change merely because its epistemic standing changes.
rows.statement: Claim/Hypothesis/Proposal are modeled as roles/modalities/epistemic standings of a common ASSERTION concept rather than as separate unrelated aggregates; example: 'the failure was caused by the database' can be the same assertion moving through HYPOTHESIS->SUPPORTED->ESTABLISHED->REJECTED without the assertion's identity changing, consistent with the existing 'identity assigned, never derived' principle.

lineage_claims.target: existing 'identity assigned, never derived' principle (assumed prior)
lineage_claims.quote: That fits beautifully with our existing: identity assigned, never derived

rows.anchor: REFERENCE ≠ QUESTION ≠ CLAIM ≠ EVIDENCE ≠ EPISTEMIC STATUS
rows.statement: Extending the Tractatus lens's sense!=truth and name/reference!=proposition/assertion distinctions (S0409), a five-way non-collapse family is proposed: Reference != Question != Claim != Evidence != Epistemic Status, described as potentially one of the most important non-collapse families discovered.

rows.anchor: Answer completeness must never be confused with question completeness.
rows.statement: The Zero lens applied to inquiry: for any answered question (e.g. WHAT happened), many companion questions (WHY, WHO had authority, WHEN was this true, WHERE does it apply, under what conditions, what evidence supports it, what would falsify it, who disputes it, what changed, what remains unknown) may have no answer at all -- 'answer completeness must never be confused with question completeness'; an AI can give a perfectly coherent answer to the wrong question.

rows.anchor: unanswered questions are not false claims
rows.statement: 'No evidence found' for the question 'Who authorized X?' must not become the claim 'Nobody authorized X' -- it must instead register as Question 'Who authorized X?' with Epistemic result UNRESOLVED, exactly the kind of silent inference the Kernel should prevent.

rows.anchor: OBJECT-LEVEL question ... META-LEVEL question
rows.statement: 'What happened?' (an object-level question producing a candidate claim) is distinguished from 'How do we know what happened?' (a meta-level question interrogating epistemic justification), giving Question->{OBJECT-LEVEL->Claim, META-LEVEL->Evidence->Justification}, connecting to prior work on justification paths and sufficiency.

rows.anchor: Which of these things must change atomically to preserve a KnowledgeOS invariant?
rows.statement: The correct DDD question for Kernel-boundary membership is reframed as 'which of these things must change atomically to preserve a KnowledgeOS invariant?' rather than 'which things are important?'; an initial candidate table places Question/Question-type/Semantic-interpretation/Reasoning/Natural-language-expression/Search-retrieval as probably outside the Kernel, and Claim identity/Hypothesis status/Evidence reference/Justification path/Authority reference/Epistemic state as potentially or already inside.

rows.anchor: What is the smallest epistemically authoritative object that the Kernel admits?
rows.statement: Recognizes that the 'candidate' the Kernel admits may itself have multiple semantic forms (Question candidate, Claim candidate, Hypothesis candidate, Evidence candidate), and explicitly declines to put all of them into the Kernel automatically -- the open question is 'what is the smallest epistemically authoritative object that the Kernel admits?'

rows.anchor: Inquiry-Assertion-Evidence-Epistemic-State separation
rows.statement: Recommendation not to change the existing Kernel boundary yet but to add a new lens-derived investigation named 'Inquiry-Assertion-Evidence-Epistemic-State separation', attacked with four tests: Test 1 Non-collapse (can Question/Claim/Evidence/Epistemic-State be distinguished without unnecessary aggregates); Test 2 Identity (does Hypothesis->Supported->Established->Superseded preserve the underlying assertion's identity); Test 3 Zero (can 'question exists, answer absent' be represented without manufacturing a negative claim); Test 4 Anti-reasoner (can the Kernel preserve question/candidate-answer/evidence/justification/epistemic-disposition without itself understanding the semantic truth of the answer).

rows.anchor: A question creates an epistemic demand; a claim proposes an answer; evidence supports or challenges the claim; justification connects the evidence to the claim; epistemic state records the governed standing of the claim.
rows.statement: Proposed as a candidate Zero-lens non-collapse finding and whiteboard-level principle: 'A question creates an epistemic demand; a claim proposes an answer; evidence supports or challenges the claim; justification connects the evidence to the claim; epistemic state records the governed standing of the claim. None of these should be silently collapsed into another.' Explicitly does not assert all six belong inside the Kernel -- that is left as the open DDD investigation.

sources.note: E1's central finding: under three-valued class-indexed Sat, 'Zero iff Delta_t=empty' names three non-equivalent predicates (Zero_strict, Zero_weak, Zero_kleene) that disagree on the most favourable case -- a fully determined, corroborated state is strict=false, weak=true, Kleene=U -- because the three universally-open classes (governance, temporal, operational) supply every U, so Zero cannot be evaluated until they are closed (Step 261's meta-gate reappearing independently). Zero_strict is unreachable in every case tested across the whole v1.2 lane.

rows.anchor: The single most consequential change is three-valued Sat: it makes v1.1's sentence "Zero <=> Delta_t = empty" ambiguous. That one sentence names three different predicates, and they disagree on the most important case.
rows.statement: States the executive finding of the v1.2 run: three-valued class-indexed Sat makes v1.1's single Zero definition name three disagreeing predicates.

rows.anchor: A state where everything the agent could determine is determined and corroborated is not Zero (strict), is Zero (weak), and undetermined (Kleene). The three undetermined requirements are governance, temporal and operational -- exactly the three classes v1.2 itself marks open.
rows.statement: Details result 1 (E1): the fully determined/corroborated case gives strict=false, weak=true, Kleene=U, and the U-producing classes are exactly the three the theory itself marks open, so Zero's evaluability is gated by the theory's own unresolved items.

sources.note: Step 189's core architectural correction: the epistemic lifecycle of a proposition requires three separate, interacting state machines (Epistemic/Governance/Operational) rather than one linear chain; includes the epistemic state set E, the Believed-is-dangerous warning, Observed!=True, Decision!=Action!=Outcome, Knowledge!=Action, and the feedback loop formula.

rows.anchor: these are not all the same kind of state
rows.statement: The naive trajectory Unknown->Observed->Believed->Supported->Determined->Decided->Refuted->Corrected mixes different semantic dimensions; the earlier single-chain state machine model is wrong and must be split.

rows.anchor: EpistemicState != GovernanceState != OperationalState
rows.statement: A proposition's lifecycle requires at minimum three distinct state dimensions -- Epistemic state E(p), Governance state G(p), and Operational state O(p) -- which must never be collapsed into one state machine; 'Decided' is a governance/action event about a proposition, not a stronger degree of knowledge about it.

rows.anchor: $$\mathcal E=\{Unknown,Observed,Hypothesized,Supported,Conflicted,Refuted,Determined,Superseded\}.$$
rows.statement: Defines the epistemic state machine's state set E = {Unknown, Observed, Hypothesized, Supported, Conflicted, Refuted, Determined, Superseded}; transitions need not move monotonically toward certainty (e.g. Supported->Conflicted or Supported->Refuted are both allowed).
missing: formal transition relation for the full state machine

rows.anchor: Therefore I would not use `Believed` as a canonical KnowledgeOS state.
rows.statement: 'Believed' is rejected as a canonical KnowledgeOS state because it conflates at least four distinct concepts (subjective belief, organizational working assumption, statistically supported hypothesis, officially accepted proposition); recommends explicit typed alternatives Belief_actor(p), WorkingAssumption(p), or Supported(p) instead, in service of DDD's precise ubiquitous language.

rows.anchor: Observed(P)\neq True(P).
rows.statement: Observation is an epistemic event, not a truth claim: Observed(P)=1 does not imply True(P)=1, because the observation itself may be wrong.

rows.anchor: Decision\neq Action\neq Outcome.
rows.statement: After a governance Decision (e.g. Upgrade), executing an Action changes operational reality (e.g. Nexus 3.69->3.70); Decision, Action, and Outcome are three distinct objects, not synonyms -- validating an (unspecified) earlier invariant.

rows.anchor: E_t\rightarrow G_t\rightarrow O_t\rightarrow E_{t+1}.
rows.statement: The complete causal/epistemic lifecycle is not one state machine but three interacting machines (Epistemic E_t, Governance G_t, Operational O_t) forming a feedback loop E_t -> G_t -> O_t -> E_{t+1}, diagrammed as Proposition -> Observation -> Evidence -> Epistemic Assessment -> {Determination | Resolution} -> Governance Decision -> Action -> Outcome -> New Observation.

rows.anchor: Refutation changes current epistemic status; it does not erase historical support.
rows.statement: When later evidence E2 demonstrates not-P after Supported(P), the state becomes Refuted(P,t2), but the original Supported(P,t1) remains historically valid -- refutation is a status change at t2, not a historical erasure.

rows.anchor: Knowledge\neq Action. And: CorrectKnowledge\neq CorrectAction without a normative layer.
rows.statement: The transition Knowledge->Action requires a Governance/NormativeRule; correct knowledge does not by itself imply correct action, which is why the architecture must not reduce organizational reasoning to statistical inference alone.

sources.note: Step 42's formal Decision Contract DC(d) and Admissible(d,K,t) predicate (Pre/Inv/Auth/Post/Temporal/Evidence, refined to P/I/A/E/Q/T/O), distinct from decision-model (the Engineering Decision Model catalog) and from decision-docket/decision-authority (ARB governance objects).

rows.anchor: How do we ensure that a KnowledgeOS decision gate can never authorize a state that violates a mandatory invariant?
rows.statement: Three distinct questions must be separated: Question 1 (Epistemic) 'Do we have sufficient knowledge?'; Question 2 (Logical) 'Are the decision conditions internally consistent?'; Question 3 (Governance/safety) 'Is the resulting action permitted?'. Therefore SufficientKnowledge != ValidDecision != AuthorizedAction. This distinction is stated as fundamental, moving the investigation from 'do we know enough' to 'is the decision formally admissible'.

rows.anchor: DC(d)=(Pre,Inv,Auth,Post,Temporal,Evidence)
rows.statement: Defines a first-version Decision Contract DC(d) = (Pre, Inv, Auth, Post, Temporal, Evidence): preconditions (what must already be true, e.g. IdentityConfirmed=True), invariants (what must never be violated, e.g. ProductionChange=>Approved, VoteCount<=MaximumAllowed, explicitly a domain constraint not merely evidence), authorization requirements, required postconditions, timing constraints, and assurance requirements. Preconditions and invariants are kept strictly separate: a precondition asks whether the world is ready for the operation; an invariant asks whether the operation is allowed to produce a state violating a protected property.

rows.anchor: {Pre(d)} d {Post(d)}
rows.statement: Borrows Hoare-logic style {P} d {Q} (if precondition P holds, execution of d should produce a state satisfying Q) and applies it as {Pre(d)} d {Post(d)}. Immediately argues ordinary Hoare logic is insufficient for KnowledgeOS because it additionally needs Evidence, Uncertainty, Authority, TemporalValidity and Provenance -- so the KnowledgeOS decision contract must extend the classical Hoare form.

rows.anchor: Admissible = Pre and Invariant and Assurance and Authorization
rows.statement: Defines Admissible(d,K,t) iff Pre(d,K,t) and Invariant(d,K,t) and Assurance(d,K,t) and Authorization(d,K,t) -- a strict conjunction. Worked example: if Pre=True, Assurance=True, Authorization=True but Invariant=False, then Admissible=False regardless; 'there must be no averaging' across the conjuncts (i.e. no compensable weighted-sum scoring of admissibility conditions).

rows.anchor: DC(d)=<P,I,A,E,Q,T,O>; Admissible as six-way conjunction
rows.statement: Restates and extends the Decision Contract as DC(d) = <P,I,A,E,Q,T,O> where P=preconditions, I=invariants, A=authorization, E=evidence requirements, Q=epistemic sufficiency, T=temporal constraints, O=postconditions; and Admissible(d,K,t) iff P(K,t) and I(K,t) and A(K,t) and E(K,t) and Q(K,t) and T(K,t), with Execute(d) only then permitted.

lineage_claims.target: the earlier DC(d)=(Pre,Inv,Auth,Post,Temporal,Evidence) definition in the same file (42.2)
lineage_claims.quote: We can now define: DC(d)= <P,I,A,E,Q,T,O>

rows.anchor: Decision evaluation != decision execution; dry-run capability
rows.statement: States that KnowledgeOS should conceptually perform Evaluate(d) before Execute(d), so Decision evaluation != Decision execution. The architecture should support Evaluate(d,K) without actually executing d, enabling simulation, review, what-if analysis, governance checks and AI planning; extends to a counterfactual decision WhatIf(Execute(d)) with estimated PostState(d), flagged as important for the later causal-reasoning formalization.

rows.anchor: Safety gate pipeline: Plan->Evaluate->Validate->Authorize->Safety Gate->Execute->Observe Outcome
rows.statement: For consequential operations, depicts a pipeline Plan -> Evaluate -> Validate -> Authorize -> Safety Gate -> Execute -> Observe Outcome, with the rule that the side effect must occur after the gate. Applies this to bound AI agents: an AI agent may propose d but should not automatically bypass Admissibility, so AIProposal -> DecisionEvaluation -> PolicyGate; states the architecture rule 'AI may propose; the governed system decides whether the proposal is admissible', and explicitly rejects Trust(AI)=True in favor of Capability(AI) constrained by Policy -- an AI agent's authority is explicitly bounded.
invariants: Capability(AI) is constrained by Policy, not by a Trust(AI)=True assumption

rows.anchor: Twelve falsification experiments for Step 42 (all PASS)
rows.statement: Runs twelve falsification tests against the Step 42 model, all recorded PASS: (1) epistemic requirements pass but authorization fails => Admissible=False; (2) authorization passes but a hard invariant fails => Block; (3) all conditions known except a safety-critical invariant => Block/Unknown per policy, never automatic authorization; (4) a valid transition from a valid state preserves the invariant; (5) a transition that would violate a domain invariant is rejected; (6) a required approval expires before execution => decision becomes inadmissible; (7) evidence used by a decision is revoked => dependency closure identifies affected assurance and decisions; (8) an AI proposes an action violating a governance rule => proposal may be recorded but execution is blocked; (9) new evidence disproves an earlier assumption => existing assurance can be downgraded/revoked; (10) a decision is evaluated without execution => dry-run result has no side effect; (11) an invariant belongs to bounded context BC_A => KnowledgeOS does not silently redefine it from BC_B; (12) a decision passes technical assurance but lacks governance authorization => TechnicallySupported=True, Authorized=False, therefore Execute=False.

experiment.hypothesis: The Step 42 decision-admissibility/safety-gate/assurance-composition model behaves correctly under twelve adversarial scenarios spanning authorization failure, invariant violation, unknown safety state, valid/invalid transitions, temporal expiry, evidence revocation, AI governance violation, non-monotonic revision, dry-run isolation, bounded-context invariant ownership, and technical-vs-governance authorization mismatch.
experiment.setup: Twelve discrete scenarios (42.49-42.60), each stating a premise and an expected outcome under the model defined in 42.1-42.48.
experiment.assumptions: The formal definitions of Admissible, Gate, invariant ownership, dependency closure and evaluate/execute separation given earlier in the same file are assumed correct.
experiment.inputs: Twelve scenario premises as listed in the statement field.
experiment.method: For each scenario, derive the expected outcome from the formal model and compare to a stated expectation.
experiment.result: All twelve scenarios PASS.
experiment.interpretation: Declared 'another major architectural milestone': KnowledgeOS moves from '(epistemically) knows enough' to 'can formally determine whether a decision is admissible'.
experiment.limitations: Falsification is by manual scenario reasoning within the document, not by an executed/automated test suite.
experiment.conclusion: STEP 42 -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Step 42 verdict and seven closing principles
rows.statement: Declares STEP 42 -- PASS and restates seven principles as the step's headline results: (1) Sufficient Knowledge != Valid Decision; (2) Valid Decision != Authorized Action; (3) Unknown safety state must not silently become safe; (4) Hard invariants are non-negotiable; (5) AI proposal != authorized execution; (6) Every consequential decision should have an explicit contract; (7) Evidence invalidation must propagate through decision dependencies.

rows.anchor: Second-order decision contract DC(d)=(Pre,Inv,Auth,Evidence,Post,Effects); horizon-dependent reachability safety; delayed effects
rows.statement: Extends the Step 42 decision contract to DC(d) = (Pre, Inv, Auth, Evidence, Post, Effects), where Effects(A) = {E_1,...,E_n} covers both ExpectedEffect and PotentialSideEffects, so the system should evaluate not only the immediate postcondition but what important downstream states an action could create. Defines horizon-dependent reachability safety: an action A is safe only if Reach_H(S,A) intersect S_unsafe = empty for horizon H -- safety cannot usually be proven for t->infinity, so a finite horizon (e.g. 24h or 30 days) must be chosen, making Safety(d,H) horizon-specific (an action safe for H=1 day may be unsafe for H=2 years). Some actions have Lag(A,Y)>0 (e.g. ArchitectureChange -> MaintenanceCost manifesting months later); represents delayed causality as Y_{t+tau}=f(A_t,...) with delay tau as part of the causal model; warns that a controller reacting before a previous action's effects become visible (A_t -> S_{t+tau} -> Decision_{t+tau+1}) can overcorrect, producing oscillation (Increase->Decrease->Increase->Decrease) even when each local decision appears rational -- 'the problem lies in the dynamic system', so the decision engine should consider EffectDelay, not merely EffectExists.

notations: representation integrity vs semantic integrity vs intent integrity
aliases: implicit information theory extracted from the Vedas/Upanishads book

sources.note: Extracts an implicit (non-Shannon) theory of information from the same Roopa Pai Vedas/Upanishads source's treatment of oral transmission, distinct from that file's knowledge-hierarchy extraction. Central claim: information is a representation transmissible between knowers but not identical with knowledge. Models the Vedic sound-based information carrier as multi-dimensional (words+pronunciation+rhythm+tone+emphasis+sequence, with Sama Veda melody notation as an encoding example), subject to transmission degradation (loss/distortion/addition/reinterpretation), for which the tradition's redundant multi-pattern recitation functioned as an error-detection/integrity mechanism (Original->multiple recitation Patterns A/B/C->cross-check->integrity). Enumerates five information channels (oral, musical, written, demonstrative, dialogical) noting the Upanishadic teacher-student form is INTERACTIVE (question-driven), not one-way broadcast. States the central distinction 'successful information transmission != successful knowledge transmission', splitting Information Transmission (Sender->Signal->Receiver) from Knowledge Transmission (Teacher->Signal->Student->Interpretation->Understanding->Experience->Realization). Adds a syntax/semantics/pragmatics decomposition of a signal, and states information is inherently contextual (Message+Context+Knower=Interpretation). Uses the historical example of ritual practice persisting after its meaning was lost (~700 BCE) as a concrete case of 'procedure preserved != purpose understood' (artifact integrity != semantic integrity), motivating a three-part integrity requirement: representation integrity (was what was said preserved), semantic integrity (was what it meant preserved), and intent integrity (was why it was said preserved). States information quality depends on the receiver, not just the message (World->Senses->Perception->Mind->Interpretation->Understanding, each stage introducing possible distortion), and that information is broader than language (linguistic/visual/auditory/behavioral/emotional/contextual/experiential), reformulated generally as 'information is a detectable difference that can alter the state of a receiver.' Concludes with a formal extracted definition ('information is a structured representation...carrying distinctions, meaning, or experience from a source to a receiver through a transmission channel; information becomes knowledge only when the receiver successfully integrates it into understanding') and a three-layer architecture (Information: representation/encoding/signal/storage/transmission/integrity -> Knowledge: meaning/context/understanding/validation/experience/reasoning -> Wisdom: judgment/action/transformation/capability/realization), plus four preserved principles: preserving information != preserving knowledge; preserving representation != preserving meaning; transmitting meaning != producing understanding; knowledge exists only when information has transformed the knower's capability.

rows.anchor: The book does not present a formal 'information theory' in the Shannon sense. ... Information is a representation of something that can be transmitted from one knower to another, but the representation is not identical with the knowledge itself.
rows.statement: Explicitly disclaims that the source presents formal Shannon-style information theory, instead extracting an implicit theory from its treatment of oral transmission: information is a transmissible representation, not identical with knowledge itself, illustrated by the Vedic sound-carrier being multi-dimensional (words+pronunciation+rhythm+tone+emphasis+sequence) rather than merely textual.

sources.note: The Gita sub-series' one genuine falsification result: Gita 13.3 textually attests Krishna as 'the knower in all fields' (a universal knower). KnowledgeOS corpus location 31.19 states an information-theoretic impossibility theorem: 'No algorithm can recover information that the observation function destroys.' A universal knower (one who could know a field regardless of what any observation function destroys) is exactly what this theorem forbids. Verdict: RX (rejected) for the universal-knower level, R5 (formally supported) for the individual-knower (kshetra-jna) level -- the source's own richer claim is refuted by independently-derived KnowledgeOS mathematics, judged more informative than an accepted analogy would have been.

rows.anchor: [S] 13.3 identifies Kṛṣṇa as the knower in all fields — a universal knower. DERIVED — KnowledgeOS has, at 31.19, an information-theoretic impossibility theorem: 'No algorithm can recover information that the observation function destroys.' A universal knower is exactly what that theorem forbids. So the source's second knower-level has no KnowledgeOS image, and the reason is mathematical. This is the lens working correctly. It offered a structure; the mathematics refused half of it; the refusal is more informative than an accepted analogy would have been. RX for the universal level, R5 for the individual one.
rows.statement: The sub-series' one clear falsification: the Gita's textually-attested universal-knower claim (13.3, Krishna as knower in all fields) is shown to be mathematically impossible under KnowledgeOS's own independently-derived information-theoretic impossibility theorem (corpus location 31.19: no algorithm can recover information an observation function has destroyed), yielding a split verdict -- RX (rejected) for the universal-knower reading, R5 (formally supported) for the individual-knower (kshetra-jna) reading -- and explicitly framed as evidence the falsification methodology is working as intended, since a genuine refutation is judged more valuable than an uncontested analogy.

sources.note: Rare executed-computational-evidence document (2026-08-30, evidence class B: two deterministic Python programs run to completion): tests the Step 222 SemanticIntegrity definition (SI(T,K,C)) against the 8 concrete scenarios and the conditional-invariant repair against all 5 minimal conflicting subsets mandated by the 20260830_935_prompts.md directive, finding SI vacuously satisfiable, non-composable (refuted by explicit counterexample), and a ternary (context-relative) relation, and correcting the verifier's own prior STEP-VERIFY-221-222.md claim that conditional invariants dissolve 4/5 MCS down to a more precise 2-dissolved/1-different-mechanism/1-relocated/1-survives breakdown.

rows.statement: Executed deterministic Python implementation of Step 222's SI(T,K,C) definition, run against all 8 scenarios mandated by the verification directive (complete preservation, partial loss undeclared, partial loss declared, AI-summary case matching SS222.14, empty critical set, contradictory declaration, ambiguous context A/B); cases 1-4 behave correctly, matching the corpus's own stated expectations.

experiment.hypothesis: Step 222's SI(T,K,C) definition is well-typed, decidable, falsifiable, useful and compositionally stable
experiment.setup: Python implementation: SI=1 if no critical distinction lost or loss is a subset of declared loss, else 0
experiment.assumptions: CriticalSemantics and Recoverable(T(K)) supplied as finite sets
experiment.inputs: 8 scenarios per the verification directive
experiment.method: execute the function on each scenario and on a two-stage composition T2∘T1
experiment.result: cases 1-4 correct; 4 defects found (see other contributions)
experiment.interpretation: SI genuinely repairs TV-F-083 but is incomplete for its own motivating use case
experiment.limitations: Recoverable(T(K)) supplied as a finite set is the favorable case; no real corpus artifact ever declares CriticalSemantics
experiment.conclusion: well-typed/decidable/falsifiable=YES; useful=PARTIALLY; stable under composition=NO

rows.anchor: CriticalSemantics(K,C) = \emptyset \Rightarrow SI = 1 for ANY transformation, including one that destroys everything.
rows.statement: Defect 1 (VACUOUS SATISFACTION, case 5): SI has no non-triviality condition on the critical-semantics set -- if CriticalSemantics(K,C) is empty, any transformation (including one that destroys everything) scores SI=1, since the declarer controls what counts as critical; identified as the same defect class as Step 100's vacuous closure theorem (TV-F-045, a universally-quantified condition over a possibly-empty set).

rows.anchor: Declaring loss of an attribute the transform actually preserves returns SI = 1 with no complaint. ... A declarer may over-declare freely
rows.statement: Defect 2 (INCOHERENT DECLARATIONS UNDETECTED, case 6): the definition never checks DeclaredLoss against what was actually lost, so a declarer may freely over-declare loss and still pass, weakening the audit value of the declaration mechanism itself.

rows.anchor: Identical K, identical T, two contexts => SI flips from 1 to 0. ... one may never say 'T preserves semantic integrity'. Only 'T preserves SI relative to C' is meaningful.
rows.statement: Defect 3 (SI IS A TERNARY RELATION, case 7): identical K and T under two different contexts flip SI from 1 to 0 -- correct by design (SI is context-relative) but with an architectural consequence the corpus does not observe: unqualified claims of the form 'T preserves semantic integrity' (found at SS218.31's Semantic Preservation Principle, SS219.25, and SS222.36's verdict, none naming C) are not well-formed under SI's own definition.

rows.anchor: SI(T1)=1 (declared Confidence) ... SI(T2)=1 (declared Source) ... SI(T2 \circ T1)=0 L={Confidence,Source} -> undeclared. ... Each stage individually satisfies semantic integrity. The composite does not.
rows.statement: Defect 4 (COMPOSITION FAILS -- the decisive result): a constructed counterexample with T1 (drops Confidence, declares it) and T2 (drops Source, declares it) each individually satisfy SI=1, but the composite T2 o T1 scores SI=0 because the corpus defines no composition rule for DeclaredLoss (it would need to union under composition); this matters because the corpus's own stated motivating case -- the AI pipeline Input->Interpretation->Summary->Recommendation (SS218.32, SS219.22) -- is exactly such a multi-stage composition, so SI as defined cannot evaluate the pipeline it was written to govern. The failure mode is identified as an instance of the corpus's own oldest theorem LocalCorrectness not-implies GlobalCorrectness (boxed at step-048 SS48.1, step-058 SS58.3, and steps 091/208/211 -- five prior boxings, none cited by Step 222's SI.

rows.anchor: Well-typed YES ... Decidable YES ... Falsifiable YES ... Useful PARTIALLY ... Stable under composition NO -- REFUTED BY EXECUTED COUNTEREXAMPLE.
rows.statement: Part 1 verdict table for SI: Well-typed YES (genuine improvement on SS215.10's ill-typed proportional-to), Decidable YES given finite CriticalSemantics/Recoverable sets, Falsifiable YES (cases 2 and 4 correctly return 0), Useful PARTIALLY (correct on design cases but vacuously satisfiable when critical=empty), Stable under composition NO (refuted by executed counterexample) -- overall: SI is a real improvement and genuine repair of TV-F-083, but incomplete in a way that defeats its own motivating use case.

rows.anchor: ESTABLISHED: 1. SI is well-typed, decidable and falsifiable ... NOT ESTABLISHED: that SI is useful at scale; that Recoverable(T(K)) is computable for real transformations ... that any declaration of CriticalSemantics exists anywhere in the corpus for any real artifact.
rows.statement: Part 3 summary of what this executed test establishes: (1) SI is well-typed/decidable/falsifiable -- TV-F-083 genuinely repaired; (2) SI is vacuously satisfiable when CriticalSemantics=empty; (3) SI does not compose, refuted by explicit counterexample, the failure being the corpus's own uncited LocalCorrectness-not-implies-GlobalCorrectness theorem; (4) SI is a ternary relation, so unqualified 'T preserves semantic integrity' statements are not well-formed; (5) conditional invariants dissolve two MCS, not four, MCS-2 survives, MCS-4 is relocated not resolved. Explicitly NOT established: that SI is useful at scale, that Recoverable(T(K)) is computable for real transformations (the finite-set case tested here is the favorable case), or that any real corpus artifact has ever actually declared a CriticalSemantics set.

rows.anchor: Add a composition rule: DeclaredLoss(T2 \circ T1) \supseteq DeclaredLoss(T1) \cup DeclaredLoss(T2). Executed test confirms this restores SI = 1 for the counterexample.
rows.statement: Part 4 (verifier-recommended, not applied, evidence class E): five possible repairs -- (1) a composition rule DeclaredLoss(T2 o T1) superset-or-equal union of DeclaredLoss(T1),DeclaredLoss(T2), executed-tested to confirm it restores SI=1 for the counterexample, rated the highest-leverage fix since without it SI cannot evaluate the AI pipeline it exists to govern; (2) a non-triviality condition barring CriticalSemantics=empty or requiring the empty declaration to be justified; (3) requiring DeclaredLoss subseteq L so over-declaration is detected; (4) always writing SI(T,K,C) with C explicit, retiring unqualified 'preserves semantic integrity' claims; (5) declaring the projection pi for MCS-1, specifying the partial order for MCS-4, naming the entropy for MCS-5, and declaring an enumerable Q for MCS-2 -- none of these repairs is established by the corpus itself.

rows.statement: Fundamental context-integration principle: distinct bounded contexts (Context_A != Context_B) can still communicate, but only through an explicit translation contract (Model_A --Translation--> Model_B), never by asserting Model_A = Model_B.

rows.anchor: An Observation is: something observed. Evidence is: an observation considered relevant to establishing or evaluating something. ... Evidence should not mutate the historical meaning of the Observation. ... Observation used as Evidence for Inquiry A / used as Evidence for Inquiry B. This is a powerful separation.
rows.statement: Worked Observation->Evidence example: 'Nexus responds on port 8081' (O1) is not automatically evidence; for the inquiry 'is Nexus reachable from application X?' it becomes E1, and it can independently become evidence for a different inquiry ('is the Nexus host running?') without mutating the historical meaning of the original observation -- illustrating Evidence as contextual rather than an intrinsic property.
invariants: Evidence must not mutate the historical meaning of the Observation

rows.anchor: Live reference: D → K_current. Historical snapshot: D → K_{t_D}. Versioned reference: D → K.v7. For auditability, the third is often stronger than a mutable live reference. But this is a design decision for a later step. ... A historical Determination must remain interpretable even if Knowledge evolves afterward. ... Interpret(D,t_D) must remain recoverable despite: K(t_D) ≠ K(t_now).
rows.statement: Identifies a major unresolved temporal design choice for how a Determination references Knowledge: live reference (D->K_current), historical snapshot (D->K_at_t_D), or versioned reference (D->K.v7) -- versioned/snapshot judged generally stronger for auditability than a mutable live reference, but explicitly deferred to a later design decision. States one of the strongest invariants derived so far: a historical Determination must remain interpretable (Interpret(D,t_D) recoverable) even though Knowledge may have since evolved (K(t_D) != K(t_now)).
missing: which reference strategy KnowledgeOS adopts is left open
invariants: Interpret(D,t_D) must remain recoverable despite K(t_D)!=K(t_now)

rows.anchor: Determination = What we conclude versus Decision = What authority chooses. This is one of the strongest conceptual boundaries in the architecture. ... AI ↓ Candidate Determination ↓ Governance Review ↓ Decision. This is much safer than: AI ↓ Decision.
rows.statement: Sharpens Determination ('what we conclude', epistemic) vs Decision ('what authority chooses', normative/authoritative) as one of the strongest conceptual boundaries derived so far; an AI-produced candidate determination must pass through governance review before becoming a decision (AI -> Candidate Determination -> Governance Review -> Decision), explicitly safer than AI -> Decision directly, since D->Decision is an input/proposal relationship, never a mutation (D not-arrow Decision_as_mutation; instead D -> DecisionProposal/Input), and governance may reject a determination (e.g. choosing DEFER or INVESTIGATE when evidence is judged insufficient) -- preserving epistemic humility.

rows.anchor: A downstream context receives the minimum semantic contract necessary to perform its responsibility. ... Projection_{GO}: GovernanceModel → OperationalCommand. The Operations context receives: ActionID Target Parameters AuthorizationReference Constraints rather than the entire Governance model.
rows.statement: Bounded-context principle: a downstream context receives the minimum semantic contract necessary to perform its responsibility, not the full upstream model -- formalized as a projection Projection_GO: GovernanceModel -> OperationalCommand, where Operations receives only ActionID/Target/Parameters/AuthorizationReference/Constraints rather than the entire Governance model. Also gives the safety property that Recommendation->Execution must never occur without passing through required governance/authorization boundaries: 'AI fluency must never substitute for authority.'
invariants: AI fluency must never substitute for authority

rows.anchor: Shared Kernel ... Customer/Supplier ... Anti-Corruption Layer ... Open Host Service ... Published Language ... For KnowledgeOS, I expect a combination of: Published Language + Anti-Corruption Layers + small Shared Kernel. The Shared Kernel should be extremely small. Likely candidates: Identity Version ProvenanceReference LineageReference ContextReference CorrelationID not the complete domain objects.
rows.statement: Reviews standard DDD context-integration patterns (Shared Kernel, Customer/Supplier, Anti-Corruption Layer, Open Host Service, Published Language) and selects a likely combination for KnowledgeOS: Published Language + Anti-Corruption Layers + a very small Shared Kernel restricted to Identity/Version/ProvenanceReference/LineageReference/ContextReference/CorrelationID (not complete domain objects); worked ACL example Decision_G --ACL--> Command_O prevents the Governance model leaking into Operations.

lexical.anchor: A bounded context owns its meaning. Therefore: Context_A ≠ Context_B does not mean they cannot communicate. It means communication must occur through an explicit contract: Model_A --Translation--> Model_B rather than: Model_A = Model_B.

formal.anchor: Observation → Evidence contextualization | Evidence → Knowledge epistemic assessment | Knowledge → Determination reasoning | Determination → Decision governance consideration | Decision → Authorization permission derivation | Authorization → Action operational command | Action → Execution realization | Execution → Observation measurement. This is much more precise than calling the entire thing a 'workflow.'

sources.note: Distinguishes Level 1 parameter uncertainty ('what is the probability?') from Level 2 model uncertainty ('are we using the right model at all?', hyperpriors), proposing a ModelValidity state (active/degrading/contradicted/superseded/context-bound/unknown) so KnowledgeOS can detect 'we may not have a bad implementation, we may have an outdated model', and represent conditional validity rather than universal truth.

rows.anchor: hyperpriors ... uncertainty about what world/model you are actually in ... repeated evidence may indicate that the environment itself has changed. ... KnowledgeOS should be able to represent: Model A: 65% / Model B: 25% / Model C: 10%.
rows.statement: Two levels of uncertainty distinguished: parameter uncertainty ('what is the probability?') versus model uncertainty ('are we using the right model at all?', hyperpriors); KnowledgeOS should represent a distribution over candidate models rather than silently committing to one, since AI systems typically hide the assumption 'my model of the problem is correct.'

rows.anchor: repeated observations can indicate that the underlying world has changed, requiring a different model rather than merely adjusting the old one. ... Model change must be detectable. ... ModelValidity: active, degrading, contradicted, superseded, context-bound, unknown.
rows.statement: ModelValidity state proposed, illustrated by an architecture decision (synchronous integration, valid under <50 req/s single-region) whose prediction errors increase after 8x traffic growth, concluding 'we may not have a bad implementation, we may have an outdated model' -- generalized into representing conditional validity rather than universal truth.

rows.anchor: 82.36 — Model uncertainty ... uncertain not only about parameters θ, but about the model itself M_1,M_2,M_3. P(D)=Σ_m P(D|M_m)P(M_m). This is model uncertainty.
rows.statement: Defines model uncertainty as uncertainty over which model (M_1,M_2,M_3,...) is correct, formalized via model averaging P(D)=Σ_m P(D|M_m)P(M_m), distinct from parameter uncertainty.

rows.statement: Experiment 18: two plausible models giving wildly different P(A) (0.9 vs 0.2) means OverallUncertainty must reflect this model-level disagreement; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.38 — Parameter uncertainty versus model uncertainty ... ParameterUncertainty from ModelUncertainty. Otherwise the system can underestimate uncertainty substantially.
rows.statement: Warns that conflating ParameterUncertainty with ModelUncertainty can cause the system to substantially underestimate total uncertainty.
